URL: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/django-vantage/rich-text/

# Rich-text fields

A rich-text field gets a small WYSIWYG editor instead of a plain textarea. The value is
stored as HTML, and that HTML is sanitised twice: when it is saved, and again every time
it is drawn.

## Which fields are rich text

Vantage treats a `TextField` as rich text when its field class name suggests it (a name
containing `richtext`, `wysiwyg`, `html` and similar) or its name ends in `_html`. Every
other `TextField` stays a plain textarea. In the JSON API and the OpenAPI document the
type is still `"richtext"` and the value is still a string.

```python
from django.db import models


class Article(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=120)
    body_html = models.TextField()      # rich text: edited in the WYSIWYG editor
    notes = models.TextField(blank=True)  # plain textarea
```

## The editor

The editor is plain JavaScript over `contenteditable`, shipped as one static file
(`vantage/vantage-richtext.js`) inside the package. There is nothing to build and no
Node.js step. It is loaded as an external script, so it works under a
Content-Security-Policy that does not allow inline scripts.

It offers bold, italic, inline code, links, a heading, bulleted and numbered lists and a
block quote. Pasting inserts plain text.

The heading, list and quote buttons replace the current block rather than nesting
inside it: a list applied to a heading turns the heading into a list, and pressing the
same button again turns the block back into a paragraph. Bold and italic are stored as
`<strong>` and `<em>`. The keyboard shortcuts are Cmd+B, Cmd+I and Cmd+K on macOS and
Ctrl+B, Ctrl+I and Ctrl+K elsewhere; the button tooltips show the one that applies. Without JavaScript the field falls back to a
textarea that holds the HTML, and the form still saves.

## What is allowed

The sanitiser uses an allowlist (it is built on the `nh3` package). Anything not named
below is removed.

| Part | Allowed |
| --- | --- |
| Tags | `p br strong b em i u s code pre blockquote ul ol li a h1`-`h6` |
| Attributes | `href` and `title` on `a`; `rel` is always set to `noopener noreferrer nofollow` |
| URL schemes | `http`, `https`, `mailto`, `tel`, and relative URLs |

Everything else is dropped: `script` and `style` elements (with their contents),
`on*` event handlers, `style` and `class` attributes, `javascript:`, `data:` and
`vbscript:` URLs, comments, forms, frames, `svg` and `math`.

Where it runs:

- **On save.** The form field cleans the submitted value, so the web forms, bulk edit,
  the CSV import and the JSON API all store sanitised HTML, whatever form-field class a
  panel's `formfield_overrides` puts on the field. (Inline cells do not edit rich text at
  all.) An editor that is emptied out
  (or whose content is entirely removed) counts as empty, so a required field still
  complains.
- **On render.** The detail page cleans the stored value before showing it, so a row
  written by a script, a migration or another application cannot put markup on the page.
  The edit form also cleans the value before it reaches the editor. Table cells show the
  visible text only, truncated.

## Widening the policy

Add to the allowlist from `settings.py`:

```python
VANTAGE = {
    # Extra tags.
    "RICHTEXT_EXTRA_TAGS": ["table", "thead", "tbody", "tr", "th", "td"],
    # Extra attributes, per tag.
    "RICHTEXT_EXTRA_ATTRIBUTES": {"td": ["colspan", "rowspan"], "th": ["colspan"]},
    # Extra URL schemes.
    "RICHTEXT_URL_SCHEMES": ["sms"],
}
```

These settings can only add. Active content cannot be switched on: `script`, `style`,
`iframe`, `object`, `embed`, `form` controls, `svg`, `math`, `template`, `noscript` and the
legacy raw-text tags (`xmp`, `noembed`, `noframes`, `plaintext`, `listing`, `marquee`);
`style`, `class`, `id`, `name`, `srcdoc`, every `on*` attribute, URL-valued attributes that
are not scheme-checked (`srcset`, `background`, `poster`, `ping`, `action`, `formaction`,
`data`, `xlink:href`) and focus or UI attributes (`autofocus`, `contenteditable`,
`tabindex`, `accesskey`, `draggable`, `is`, `slot`), including through the `*` key; and the `javascript`, `data`,
`vbscript`, `blob` and `file` schemes. Asking for one raises `ImproperlyConfigured` the
first time settings are read. The editor itself only produces the default tags, so extra
tags are for HTML you load from elsewhere and want to keep.

## Keeping the markdown toolbar

Some fields already hold markdown, not HTML. Two ways to keep the older plain textarea
with a markdown toolbar for them:

```python
from vantage.panels import ModelPanel


class ArticlePanel(ModelPanel):
    # These fields are stored and shown exactly as typed. They are not sanitised as
    # HTML, and they are escaped, never interpreted, when displayed.
    markdown_fields = ("body_html",)
```

Or for every rich-text field in the project:

```python
VANTAGE = {"RICHTEXT_EDITOR": "markdown"}   # default: "html"
```

Existing content in an HTML field is shown as it is, after sanitising. Content that is
plain text or markdown opens in the HTML editor as literal text, so use `markdown_fields`
for fields that hold markdown.

---

URL: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/django-vantage/undo/

# Undo

After a delete or an edit, the confirmation toast carries an **Undo** button:

> Deleted 3 orders. (3 selected records) · **Undo**

It stays for `VANTAGE["UNDO_WINDOW"]` seconds (10 by default), and pressing it — or
<kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>⌘</kbd>+<kbd>Z</kbd> while you are not typing in a field — puts the
records back. There is nothing to configure: every panel gets it.

![The Undo toast after deleting a review](assets/screenshots/undo-light.webp){ .dv-shot .dv-only-light }
![The Undo toast after deleting a review](assets/screenshots/undo-dark.webp){ .dv-shot .dv-only-dark }

```python
VANTAGE = {
    "UNDO_WINDOW": 10,      # seconds; 0 turns undo off everywhere
    "UNDO_MAX_ROWS": 1000,  # larger changes still happen, without an Undo
}

@register(Payout)
class PayoutPanel(ModelPanel):
    undo = False            # this model's deletes and edits are final
```

The feature exists to stop data being lost, so it is built around one rule: **an undo
that might restore the wrong thing is never offered**. In those cases the change happens
exactly as it always did and the toast simply has no button. Everything below is what
that rule means in practice.

## What can be undone

| Change | How it is reversed |
|---|---|
| Delete (record page) | Soft delete: un-trashed. Hard delete: snapshot and restore |
| Delete (bulk, `actions = ["delete_selected"]`) | The same, for every selected row |
| Bulk edit | Each row's previous values are written back |
| Inline cell edit | The same, and the grid updates in place without a reload |
| Publish / Unpublish (built-in) | The flag goes back to what it was, row by row |
| Your own `@action` | Only if it declares how — see [below](#undo-for-your-own-actions) |

`delete_selected` is the bulk counterpart of the Delete page, and opt-in:

```python
class OrderPanel(ModelPanel):
    actions = ["mark_paid", "delete_selected"]
```

On a model with a trash it trashes, exactly like the per-record button; inside the
trash it deletes for good. It needs the `delete` permission, confirms first, and one
`PROTECT` reference anywhere in the selection leaves every row as it was.

## Edits: only if nobody has touched it since

An edit records each row's values before and after, read back from the database inside
the transaction that wrote them. Undo writes the "before" back **only if every row still
holds exactly the "after"** — checked under a row lock. If a colleague has changed one of
those fields since, nothing is reverted at all, and the toast says so:

> 1 record has been changed by someone else since, so nothing was undone. Their change has
> been kept.

All or nothing, deliberately. Reverting nine rows and skipping the tenth leaves a state
nobody chose; reverting the tenth would destroy someone else's work. The undo also
advances the [optimistic-lock](lists.md) version column, so an edit form somebody has
open on the old values conflicts rather than quietly writing them back.

An edit is not offered for undo when it touches a field whose value cannot be compared
and restored faithfully — a file, a JSON field, a binary field or a many-to-many.

## Soft deletes: already reversible

When the model has a trash (a `deleted_at` timestamp or an `is_deleted` flag — see
[Inference](inference.md)), Delete marks the row and Undo unmarks it, on the condition
that the mark is still the one this delete wrote.

## Hard deletes: snapshot and restore

The delete runs immediately, as it always has, inside one transaction that first records
every row the cascade is about to remove — and the old value of every foreign key that
`SET_NULL` or `SET_DEFAULT` will rewrite. Undo re-inserts those rows with their original
primary keys, many-to-many rows included, and points those foreign keys back.

### Why not "deferred delete"?

The other common design keeps the rows, hides them, and deletes them when the window
closes. It was rejected:

* **Hiding only works inside the admin.** Your site, your API, your workers and your
  reports would keep reading — and writing — records the user was told were gone.
* **Somebody has to run the delete later.** With several worker processes and no
  guaranteed scheduler, a deletion can run late or never. For a record deleted for
  privacy reasons, *never* is the failure that matters.
* **The delete would run against data that has moved.** A new `PROTECT` reference makes
  it fail after the user was told it succeeded; a new `CASCADE` child is destroyed without
  ever having been shown on the confirmation page.

### When a hard delete has no Undo

Snapshot and restore has risks of its own. Each is a case where the delete proceeds
normally and no Undo is offered:

| Condition | Why |
|---|---|
| A `pre_delete`/`post_delete` receiver on any model in the cascade | It may have deleted a file, revoked a key or called an external service. Re-inserting the row cannot reverse that, and would resurrect a record pointing at things that no longer exist |
| A database-level `on_delete` (`DB_CASCADE`, `DB_SET_NULL`…) touching the cascade | The database rewrites rows the snapshot never saw |
| The model overrides `delete()`, or its default queryset overrides `QuerySet.delete()` | Your own delete has to run, and it cannot be snapshotted from outside |
| More than `UNDO_MAX_ROWS` rows, cascade and rewritten references included | The snapshot itself would be the problem |
| A binary column in the cascade | Not snapshotted |

Restoring is just as careful. Rows are inserted with `force_insert`, so a primary key or
a unique value somebody has taken in the meantime is an error, never an overwrite; a
`SET_NULL` reference somebody has since pointed elsewhere is a conflict; foreign-key
integrity is checked before commit. Any failure rolls the whole restore back and says
that nothing was changed.

Restored rows are saved with `raw=True`, exactly as `loaddata` saves fixtures, so
`pre_save`/`post_save` receivers see them — check `raw` if a receiver should ignore them.

## The token

Each Undo carries a random token that is:

* **single-use** — consumed by a conditional `UPDATE` before anything is restored, so a
  double click undoes once and both clicks get the same answer;
* **bound to the user and to the browser session** that made the change;
* **short-lived** — it expires with the window, and the server enforces that whatever the
  page shows;
* **as privileged as the change** — undoing a delete needs `delete`, undoing an edit needs
  `change`, re-checked at the moment of the undo, and refused in read-only mode;
* **redeemed only by a CSRF-protected POST** to `<site>/_/undo/`;
* **audit-logged** — a successful undo writes "undid delete of 3 orders" to the
  [audit log](permissions.md).

Only a hash of the token is stored. Entries live in the `vantage_undoentry` table;
expired ones are purged whenever a new one is written, each user keeps at most twenty,
and a redeemed entry drops its snapshot immediately. A hard delete's snapshot is a copy
of deleted data, so if you need a firm bound on how long it can outlive its window, run
`manage.py vantage_purge_undo` from cron.

## Undo for your own actions

An action is arbitrary code, so its inverse is never guessed. Say which fields it writes
and Vantage records and restores them, with the same conflict check as an edit:

```python
@action("Mark as paid", bulk_strategy="sql", undo_fields=["status"])
def mark_paid(self, request, queryset):
    return f"{queryset.update(status='paid')} orders marked paid."
```

For anything `undo_fields` cannot express, return the state you will need and name a
hook. The hook runs inside a transaction; raise `UndoConflict` to refuse, and everything
it did is rolled back:

```python
from vantage.actions import ActionResult
from vantage.undo import UndoConflict

@action("Refund", undo="undo_refund")
def refund(self, request, queryset):
    ids = list(queryset.values_list("pk", flat=True))
    queryset.update(status="refunded")
    return ActionResult(f"Refunded {len(ids)}.", undo_state={"ids": ids})

def undo_refund(self, request, state):
    rows = Order.objects.filter(pk__in=state["ids"], status="refunded")
    if rows.count() != len(state["ids"]):
        raise UndoConflict("Some of these orders have moved on since the refund.")
    rows.update(status="paid")
```

Actions large enough to run as a [background job](lists.md#background-jobs) never offer
undo: there is no toast to put the button in.

## Accessibility and no-JavaScript

The toast region is a `role="status"` live region, so the message and its button are
announced. The Undo button is an ordinary focusable `<button>`, it declares its shortcut
with `aria-keyshortcuts`, and the shortcut follows the same on/off switch as the grid's
keyboard shortcuts. The toast does not steal focus. Its entrance animation is dropped
under `prefers-reduced-motion`.

Without JavaScript the button is never shown, and every change behaves exactly as it did
before undo existed: a button that could outlive its own window would be a promise the
page cannot keep.

---

URL: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/django-vantage/history/

# History

Every record has a **History** page, linked from the history panel on its detail page
("As it was…"). It lists everything the [audit log](permissions.md#the-audit-log) holds
for the record, and shows the record **as it was at any point** in that list — field by
field, next to how it is now. From there you can **restore** some or all of those
fields.

```
/admin/shop/order/42/history/                       the timeline
/admin/shop/order/42/history/?entry=318             as it was just after entry 318
/admin/shop/order/42/history/?at=2026-03-01T09:30   as it was at that moment
```

There is nothing to configure: every panel gets it while the audit log is on.

```python
@register(Payout)
class PayoutPanel(ModelPanel):
    history = "view"        # show the history, but never offer to restore from it

@register(Invoice)
class InvoicePanel(ModelPanel):
    history = False         # no history page for this model
```

## How a value is worked out

Each change the log records carries the value it replaced and the value it wrote.
Starting from the record as it stands now, the page walks those changes backwards to
the point you chose.

That only tells the truth about changes made **through the panel**. The audit log is
not row history: a script, an import, a data migration or a `shell` session writes
nothing to it. So a value is only shown as known when the log is consistent with
itself — every change's "from" matches the previous change's "to", and the last "to"
matches what the record holds today. If something the panel never saw moved the field
in between, the chain breaks, and the page says the value **cannot be worked out**
instead of showing what the surviving half of the chain suggests.

Every field comes back with one of these verdicts, written out on the page:

| Verdict | Shown | Restorable |
|---|---|---|
| Known, same as now | Yes | Nothing to restore |
| Known, different from now | Yes | Yes |
| Recorded only approximately (a JSON value, a many-to-many, a text clipped at 500 characters) | Yes, with the reason | No |
| Not confirmed, because a bulk change ran since (see below) | Yes, with the reason | No |
| Cannot be worked out (changed outside the panel) | No | No |
| A foreign key or a file | No | No |
| A [sensitive field](sensitive-fields.md) | Masked | No |

## What it cannot reconstruct

Being clear about this is the feature, so here it is in full.

* **Anything before the record's history starts.** If the record existed before the
  audit log was switched on — or before it was first edited through the panel — the
  page says where its history begins and shows nothing earlier. Before a record's
  *create* entry it says the record did not exist yet.
* **Fields that are not inputs on the edit form.** The log only records what the form
  wrote, so an `auto_now` timestamp, a non-editable column, and anything in `exclude` or
  `readonly_fields` has no history at all. They are listed under the table rather than
  shown with today's value as if it were the old one. If you have changed a panel's
  form fields over time, the history follows what each edit's form contained.
* **Foreign keys.** The log records a relation by its label, not by which record it
  pointed to, so there is nothing that could be written back.
* **Files and binary values.** A file is recorded by name only, never its contents; a
  binary column is never recorded.
* **JSON, many-to-many and very long text.** Recorded approximately — list order is not
  kept, a long text is clipped — so they are shown but never restored.
* **Sensitive fields.** Never shown, then or now, and never restored. The diff never
  carried their values in the first place, and an entry written before the field was
  declared sensitive is masked too.
* **Bulk actions.** A bulk action, a one-statement bulk edit and an undo are logged once
  per run, not once per record, so the record's own history cannot say whether one of
  them touched it. When one ran after the point you chose, the page says so, and any
  field it could have touched is shown as *not confirmed* unless an entry at or before
  that point confirms it.
* **Deep history.** The page replays at most the record's 2,000 most recent entries.

## Restoring

Tick the fields you want back and press **Restore selected fields**. A restore is an
ordinary edit:

* It needs the `change` permission on the record, rechecked when you press the button,
  and it is refused in [read-only mode](settings.md).
* It saves through the panel's own edit form — the same validation, the same
  `save_model` hook, the same [tenancy](tenancy.md) guard. If an old value is no longer
  accepted (a choice has been removed, a unique value has since been taken by another
  record), nothing is saved and the page says why.
* It is refused if the record has changed since you opened the page: by the
  [optimistic lock](lists.md) on a model that has one, and otherwise by comparing the
  current values the page was drawn with. A colleague's newer change is never rolled
  back by accident.
* It writes its own [audit entry](permissions.md#the-audit-log) — an update with the
  usual diff, marked "restored as of" the point you chose. That entry is itself part of
  the history, so a restore can be looked back past, and restored from, like any other
  change.

The values themselves never travel through the browser. The page posts back only
*which* fields to restore and the point to restore them from; the server works the
values out again from the log, so a hand-written request cannot restore a field to
anything the history does not say it held.

## Who can see it

Two permissions, because the page answers two questions:

* **What the record held** needs `view` on that record, checked the way every record
  page checks it — a record outside your scope is a 404.
* **Who changed it** is the audit log's own question, so the page also needs what the
  log needs: a superuser, or the `vantage.view_vantagelogentry` permission. Without it
  the detail page shows no history panel and the history page is refused.

Restoring additionally needs `change`, and `history = "view"` turns restoring off for
everyone.

## When you need row history

The log is "what people did in the panel". If you need every write from every source —
workers, imports, the shell — install
[django-simple-history](https://django-simple-history.readthedocs.io/); its timeline
renders next to Vantage's own on the detail page.

---

URL: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/django-vantage/approvals/

# Approvals

Some fields need a second pair of eyes. Name them on the panel:

```python
@register(Product)
class ProductPanel(ModelPanel):
    requires_approval = ["price", "status"]
```

That is the whole configuration. Anyone who may change a product still can. When
someone who **cannot approve** changes `price`, every other field they changed is saved
as usual, and the new price becomes a **change request**: who asked, when, the value
they saw, the value they want, and an optional note. The product keeps its old price
until someone who **can approve** says yes.

```
/admin/_/approvals/          the queue: waiting for you, your requests, recently decided
/admin/_/approvals/12/       one request: what it is now, what was asked, approve or reject
```

## Who may approve

Superusers, and anyone holding the model's approve permission:

```
shop.approve_product
```

It is named the way Django names the other four (`get_permission_codename("approve",
opts)`), and it is created for every panel that sets `requires_approval` when you run
`migrate` — no `Meta.permissions` and no migration in your app. It appears in that
model's row of the [roles matrix](roles.md), next to view, add, change and delete.

Approving writes the record, so it also needs **change** permission on it. A panel can
answer for itself, the same way it does for the other verbs:

```python
def has_approve_permission(self, request, obj=None):
    return request.user.groups.filter(name="Finance").exists()
```

Someone who may approve changes these fields directly: their edits are not held, the
same as before. Read-only mode (`VANTAGE["READ_ONLY"]`) refuses approving, rejecting and
withdrawing along with every other write.

**Nobody approves their own request — superusers included.** A superuser's own edits
are never held in the first place, so in practice this only stops someone who was
given the approve permission after asking. "I asked, and then I said yes" is exactly
what the feature exists to rule out.

## What the person editing sees

The edit page says which fields will wait before anything is typed, and offers a box
for a note to the approver. After saving, the message says what was saved and what was
sent for approval; if the only change was to a held field, it does not say "saved".

The record's detail and edit pages show a banner while a change to it is waiting: the
field, the value now, the value asked for, who asked and when. Anyone who can see the
record sees it. The **Review** link only appears for someone who could act on it.

## Approving, and when it is stale

The review screen shows each field's value when the request was made, the value asked
for, and — if it has moved since — what it is now.

**Approve** saves the change through the same path as an edit: the panel's form
validates it again, `save_model` runs, [tenancy](tenancy.md) is enforced, and the audit
entry and the `updated` [webhook](webhooks.md) happen then — at the moment the record
actually changes, with the approver as the actor.

Each request carries the value its author saw. If the field has changed since — someone
else edited it, or another request was approved first — the request is **stale**: it no
longer means what it said, so it is not applied. The page marks the field and shows its
current value. Reject it, and the author asks again from the record as it now is. A
request is never applied over a newer value.

If the requested value is no longer acceptable — a choice that has been removed, a
unique value taken since — nothing is saved and the request stays pending, to be
rejected.

**Reject** needs a reason, which the requester sees on the queue. **Withdraw** is the
requester taking their own request back. Each of the three is one conditional update,
so two people pressing at once produce one decision and one "already decided".

## Every way to change a record

| Path | What happens to a held field |
|---|---|
| Edit page | Held; the rest of the form saves |
| [History](history.md) restore | Held, like an edit; the message counts only what was restored |
| Inline cell editing | Held; the rest of the row saves, the cell shows the stored value and the bar says why |
| Kanban move | Held; the card goes back to its column with a note on it |
| [JSON API](api.md) `PUT`/`PATCH` | Held; answers **202** with the stored record and a `pending` object |
| [Import](lists.md) (update rows) | Held **per record**; counted as "sent for approval" in the preview and the result |
| Bulk edit | **Refused** when a held field is ticked, before anything is written |
| Built-in Publish/Unpublish, and any action whose `undo_fields` name a held field | **Not offered** to someone whose change would be held |
| Creating a record | Not held — there is no approved value to protect yet |

The bulk paths refuse rather than queue because a bulk edit can be one `UPDATE` over
forty thousand rows. That cannot be held back row by row, and forty thousand requests
would bury the queue the feature depends on. The message names the field and says to
change it one record at a time.

An import is different: every row already goes through its own form and its own
save, so each one queues like an edit would. A dry run shows how many would be sent
for approval and leaves nothing behind.

Over the API, a client can tell in advance: the [schema](api.md) marks each field with
`needs_approval` for the caller asking. A held write answers:

```json
HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted

{
  "pk": 42, "fields": {"price": "10.00", "...": "..."},
  "pending": {
    "id": 12,
    "status": "pending",
    "fields": ["price"],
    "requested": {"price": "12.50"},
    "detail": "Your change to Price was sent for approval. ..."
  }
}
```

Send `"note"` beside `"fields"` to leave one for the approver.

## The queue

The **Approvals** page is in the System group of the navigation for anyone who can view
a model that sets `requires_approval`. It has three parts:

- **Waiting for you** — pending requests you may decide, oldest first. The number
  beside the page in the navigation is how many there are.
- **Your requests** — what you asked for, and what became of it.
- **Recently decided** — for approvers, the last twenty decisions.

A request is exactly as visible as its record. Every lookup goes through the panel's
scoped queryset — `PanelPermissions.filter_queryset`, which is also where
[tenancy](tenancy.md) is applied — so a request about a record you cannot see is not in
your queue, not in your count, and answers 404 by its id. The one exception is your
own request whose record you can no longer reach: you can still read it and withdraw
it.

## Sensitive fields

A [sensitive field](sensitive-fields.md) can be held like any other, and it stays
masked on the queue, on the review screen, in the banner and in the API's `pending`
object — on both sides. An approver who may reveal values does so on the record itself,
where the reveal is logged.

The value asked for has to be stored to be applied, so it is kept on the request row,
as the record itself keeps the current one. The request table is not offered as a
model in the panel.

## With field permissions

[Field permissions](field-permissions.md) apply to approvals the way they apply
everywhere else, plus one rule about deciding:

- **A field hidden from you is never named or shown** on the queue, the review screen,
  the record's banner or in the API. A request that touches one shows its other fields
  and one more row, "1 field you cannot see", with no name and no values. Its note and
  rejection reason are left out too, since they are free text about those values. This
  holds for the requester as well, if a role has hidden a field since they asked.
- **A read-only field cannot be asked for.** Every path refuses it before the approval
  hold is reached: the edit page and duplicate show it as text and ignore a forged
  value, inline editing and the board do not offer it, the API answers **400**, import
  does not map it and history restore does not offer it. The edit page's "needs
  approval" note and the schema's `needs_approval` only name fields you may write.
- **Deciding needs write access to every field in the request.** Approving changes the
  fields, so an approver for whom any of them is hidden or read-only cannot approve
  *or* reject that request. It is not under "Waiting for you" and not in the count; the
  review screen, if they open it, says why. Someone else, whose roles let them change
  every field in it, decides it. A superuser always can.
- **A request is applied whole or not at all.** Approving never drops a field the
  approver may not write: it is refused, with that reason, before anything is saved.

The audit entries below name the request's fields. Someone a field is hidden from reads
`requested approval of status, 1 hidden field (#12)` instead, on the history page, the
audit log and the record's history panel, and the approval's diff leaves the field out,
as every diff does.

## What is audited

| When | Entry |
|---|---|
| A change is held | `action` — `requested approval of price (#12)` |
| It is approved | `update` — the real diff, `approved change to price (#12)`, by the approver |
| It is rejected | `action` — `rejected change to price (#12)` |
| It is withdrawn | `action` — `withdrew request to change price (#12)` |

Only the approval is an `update` with a diff, so the record's [history](history.md) and
its webhooks see the change once, when it happens. The other entries carry no values;
those live on the request, where the reason and the note are too. When an edit both
changes ordinary fields and holds one, its own `update` entry lists only the fields
that were saved.

## Checks

`manage.py check` names every entry that cannot be held, because at runtime such an
entry is skipped — and a field you meant to protect would then save directly:

| Id | Problem |
|---|---|
| `vantage.E105` | `requires_approval` is not a list of field names |
| `vantage.E106` | It names something that is not a field of the model |
| `vantage.E107` | It names a field the panel's form does not let anyone edit |
| `vantage.E108` | It names a many-to-many, a reverse relation or a file field |

Many-to-many values are written after the row and files are stored as they are saved,
so neither can wait for approval.

## Limits

Said plainly, because a control that looks stronger than it is does harm:

- **Only what goes through the panel.** A management command, a data migration, a
  `shell` session or your own view writing the model directly is not held. This is a
  review step in the admin, not a database constraint.
- **Your own actions.** A custom `@action` that writes a held field with
  `queryset.update()` is only kept from non-approvers when it lists that field in
  `undo_fields`. Otherwise, check `vantage.approvals.guarded_for(request, panel)` in it.
- **Creating** a record is not held; the add permission is the gate for that.
- **A deleted record** takes its pending requests out of everyone's queue but their
  author's, who can still withdraw them.

---

URL: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/django-vantage/pages-and-dashboards/

# Pages and dashboards

[← Index](index.md)

Two escape hatches from the model-shaped world: a screen that is not a model, and the
landing page that greets everyone.

## Custom pages

A reporting screen, an operations console, a settings form. The bar this API has to
clear is that adding one should feel no heavier than writing a `ModelPanel` — a class, a
title, and a method that returns some data.

```python
# ops/panel.py
from vantage import Page, site

from shop.models import Order


@site.register_page
class RevenuePage(Page):
    title = "Revenue"
    icon = "trending-up"

    def get_context(self, request):
        return {"total": Order.objects.total_revenue()}
```

Everything else has a default. The URL comes from the class name, the nav entry appears
on its own, and the template falls back to a generic renderer that displays whatever
`get_context` returned — so a page with no template at all still produces a presentable
screen, which is what keeps the first one cheap to write.

### Attributes

| Attribute | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | the slug, prettified | Nav label and page heading |
| `description` | `""` | A line under the heading |
| `icon` | `None` | Lucide icon name |
| `group` | `"Pages"` | Which sidebar group it sits in |
| `order` | `0` | Sorts the group |
| `path` | `"<slug>/"` | URL segment, relative to where the site is mounted |
| `slug_override` | `None` | An explicit slug, if the derived one is not what you want |
| `permission` | `None` | A permission string, or a callable taking the request |
| `template_name` | `None` | Falls back to `vantage/pages/<slug>.html`, then `vantage/page.html` |

### Slugs and URLs

The trailing `Page` is dropped, because every class has it and repeating it in every URL
would be noise, and CamelCase becomes hyphens.

```pycon
>>> class RevenueReportPage(Page): ...
>>> RevenueReportPage.get_slug()
'revenue-report'
>>> RevenueReportPage.get_path()
'revenue-report/'
```

Reverse it as `vantage:page-<slug>` — `reverse("vantage:page-revenue-report")`.

A page with nothing declared at all still works:

```pycon
>>> class BarePage(Page): ...
>>> BarePage.get_slug(), BarePage.get_title()
('bare', 'Bare')
>>> BarePage().get_template_names()
['vantage/pages/bare.html', 'vantage/page.html']
```

Custom pages are routed **before** model routes, so a page may deliberately claim a path
that would otherwise look like an app prefix.

### Permissions

```python
class PayoutsPage(Page):
    permission = "finance.view_payout"           # a Django permission string


class BetaPage(Page):
    permission = staticmethod(lambda request: request.user.email.endswith("@acme.com"))
```

A callable receives the request, so a page can be gated on anything — a feature flag,
group membership, the time of day — without inventing a permission just to express it.

The nav consults the same gate, so a page you cannot open is not listed. Listing a page
that 403s on click is a worse experience than omitting it, and for a page gated on
something sensitive the label itself can be a disclosure.

### Templates

Extend Vantage's base to inherit the chrome:

```html
{% extends "vantage/base.html" %}

{% block content %}
  <h1>{{ page.get_title }}</h1>
  <p>{{ total }}</p>
{% endblock %}
```

Or supply nothing at all and let `vantage/page.html` render `get_context`'s return
value.

### The built-in pages

Four pages are registered by the app config rather than left for projects to add,
because they are only useful if they are always there — one you have to switch on is one
you never remember exists.

| Page | Path | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Schema | `/_/schema/` | anyone who can reach the panel |
| System | `/_/health/` | superusers only |
| Data quality | `/_/data-quality/` | superusers, unless `DATA_QUALITY["PERMISSION"]` widens it — see [Data quality](data-quality.md) |
| Roles | `/_/roles/` | superusers, unless `ROLES_PERMISSION` widens it; only with `django.contrib.auth` — see [Roles](roles.md) |

All four register **before** autodiscovery, so a project can unregister or replace one from
its own `panel.py`.

The **schema map** is derived from the registry at request time, so it is always
current, and every node is a link — seeing that Orders point at Customers and clicking
straight through is a different act from reading a picture. The layout is computed in
Python rather than by a JavaScript graph library: a schema graph is tens of nodes, not
thousands, and a server-side layered layout means the page needs no JavaScript, works
with the print stylesheet, and cannot flash. Models the user cannot view are omitted.

```pycon
>>> graph = build_graph(site, request)
>>> len(graph.nodes), len(graph.edges)
(9, 9)
```

The **system page** is covered under [Deployment](deployment.md#the-system-page).

## Dashboards

A dashboard is a class with a method, exactly like a page.

```python
# shop/dashboard.py
from django.db.models import Avg, Count, Sum

from shop.models import Order, Product, Review
from vantage import Chart
from vantage.dashboards import (
    ChartCard, Dashboard, ListCard, StatCard, TableCard, TemplateCard,
)


class ShopDashboard(Dashboard):
    title = "Overview"
    description = "Six months of trading, computed on request."

    def get_widgets(self, request):
        return [
            StatCard("Revenue", Order.objects.exclude(status="refunded"),
                     aggregate=Sum("total"), format="currency", trend="created_at"),
            StatCard("Orders", Order.objects.all(), trend="created_at"),
            StatCard("Average order", Order.objects.all(),
                     aggregate=Avg("total"), format="currency"),
            StatCard("Refunded", Order.objects.filter(status="refunded"),
                     tone="destructive"),
            ChartCard("Revenue over time", Order.objects.all(),
                      chart=Chart.timeseries("Revenue", date="created_at",
                                             value=Sum("total"))),
            ChartCard("Orders by status", Order.objects.all(),
                      chart=Chart.breakdown("Orders", group_by="status",
                                            value=Count("id"), kind="donut")),
            TableCard("Latest orders", Order.objects.all(), limit=5),
            TableCard("Newest reviews", Review.objects.select_related("product"),
                      columns=["headline", "product", "rating"], limit=5),
            ListCard("Catalogue", lambda request: [
                ("Products", Product.objects.count()),
                {"label": "Out of stock",
                 "value": Product.objects.filter(stock=0).count(),
                 "tone": "warning"},
            ]),
            TemplateCard("Five-star reviews", "shop/_five_star.html"),
        ]
```

Point at it:

```python
VANTAGE = {"DASHBOARD": "shop.dashboard.ShopDashboard"}
```

That is the demo's dashboard, and it renders ten cards.

### Widgets

| Widget | Default width | |
|---|---|---|
| `StatCard(label, source, aggregate=None, format="number", tone=None, trend=None, currency="$")` | 1 | One number over a queryset |
| `ChartCard(label, source, chart=Chart…)` | 2 | One chart, drawn as server-side SVG |
| `TableCard(label, source, columns=None, limit=5, order_by=None)` | 2 | The most recent handful of records, linked |
| `ListCard(label, items)` | 1 | Arbitrary label/value pairs |
| `TemplateCard(label, template_name, context=None)` | 2 | Your own template inside a card |

Every widget also takes `width` (1 to 4 — the grid is four columns), `permission`,
`description`, `url` and `icon`.

```pycon
>>> StatCard("Too wide", Order.objects.all(), width=9)
ValueError: Widget 'Too wide' declares width 9; the dashboard grid is 4 columns wide,
            so width must be 1 to 4.
```

`StatCard`'s aggregate defaults to a row count, because that is what most of the first
cards on any dashboard are and it should not have to be spelled out.

`TableCard` is deliberately short and unpaginated: a glance at what just happened with a
way through to the list page, not a second list page. Its columns default to the
model's inferred ones, capped at four, and it renders cells through the model's
registered panel, so your own cell formatting applies. `select_related` is planned from
those columns — five rows with a relation column is still five extra queries otherwise,
and a dashboard is the page most likely to hold several of these at once.

`ListCard` items are `(label, value)` pairs or dicts with `label` / `value` and optional
`url` and `tone`.

The `source` of a queryset widget may be a **queryset**, a **manager**, or a
**callable** returning one. A callable is the escape hatch for anything that depends on
the request, and it may take `request` or no arguments at all — `Order.objects.all` and
`lambda request: …` are equally natural things to write.

### Four load-bearing properties

**Nothing is computed at import time.** Widgets are declarations; the queryset a widget
holds is never evaluated until the dashboard renders inside a request. A module-level
queryset is re-cloned per request with `.all()`, so it cannot cache its rows the first
time it is iterated and serve that snapshot to every later request — the classic
module-level-queryset bug.

**A widget the user may not see never runs its query.** The permission gate is checked
*before* the card is rendered, not after. A card that computes a number and then hides it
has already leaked it into the query log and paid for it. A queryset widget infers its
model from its source, so it is gated on the same `view` permission the model's own
pages are, and can never become a side channel around the sidebar. A callable source
cannot be inspected without running it — and running user code to decide whether the
user may run it is backwards — so those widgets declare `model=` or `permission=`.

Every queryset also passes through `filter_queryset`, so a number computed over rows you
cannot list is not a leak.

**Widgets fail independently.**

```pycon
>>> D(site).render(request)          # one card has a broken aggregate
[('Broken', error=True), ('Fine', error=False)]
```

An exception inside one card renders that card as an error and leaves its neighbours
intact. A dashboard that 500s because one team's custom aggregate broke is a dashboard
nobody trusts.

**Aggregation is not reimplemented here.** Every number and every chart goes through the
same code the [list page's analytics](analytics.md) use, so the dashboard inherits its
formatting, its trend windows and its join-fanout correctness for free.

Dashboard cards are **never budgeted**. The [budget gate](analytics.md#the-budget)
belongs to the list page, where analytics are chrome above the thing the user came for.
A dashboard *is* the thing the user came for.

### The default dashboard

Zero configuration is the package's thesis, so the default cannot be a placeholder.
Declare no `DASHBOARD` and you get:

- a **count card** for every model you may see, in registry order so the cards read in
  the same order as the sidebar (capped at 12);
- a **timeseries of new records** for the most interesting model that stamps a creation
  date;
- a **recent-records table** for up to three such models.

```pycon
>>> DefaultDashboard(site).render(request)
13 cards: Groups, Users, Categories, Customers, Orders, Order items, Products,
          Reviews, Tags, New orders (chart), Recent orders, Recent products,
          Recent reviews
```

Two details.

**Permission filtering happens before the cap.** Capping first would mean a user who can
see only one model, and whose model sorts outside the first twelve, gets an entirely
empty dashboard — the cap would silently have become an access rule.

**Framework apps sort last for the space-hungry cards.** `admin`, `auth`,
`contenttypes`, `sessions` and `vantage` still get a count card, but a chart of user
signups on a two-account project is a flat line where the project's own orders would
have been a shape.

The "when was this created" field is found separately from the timeline pattern
detector, because they answer different questions: the detector picks the best field to
*group by* and therefore prefers a domain date such as `published_at`, while "recent
records" and "new per week" need the date the row came into existence. `auto_now_add` is
proof of that and wins outright.

```pycon
>>> creation_field(Order), creation_field(Product), creation_field(Customer)
('created_at', 'created_at', 'joined_on')
```

A nullable date is no good here — half the rows would fall outside every bucket — so it
is refused.

## Arranging the dashboard from the UI

Everything above is the *code* layer. `?arrange=1` puts the dashboard into an editing
mode with a row underneath that code, following the same shape
[the per-list customisation rail](lists.md#the-customisation-rail) and
[`vantage.listprefs`](configuration.md#the-same-shape-wherever-it-appears)
established first:

```
per-user row  >  site-wide row  >  VANTAGE["DASHBOARD"]  >  DefaultDashboard
```

A stored arrangement is a list of entries, and each entry is one of two things: a
pointer at a card the code already declares — by key, so the declaration stays the
source of what the card *means* while the row only says where it sits, how wide it is
and whether it currently shows — or a card someone built entirely in the UI, over any
model they may view.

### Building a card without writing Python

The "Add a card" picker offers exactly two shapes — a stat or a chart, not the table
and list cards, which need columns and hand-written pairs no picker can meaningfully
ask for. Choosing a model, an aggregate (count, sum, average, min, max), a column to
aggregate over, and — for a chart — a date field to bucket by or a low-cardinality
column to break down by, produces a card that runs through exactly the same
`vantage.stats.compute_panel` every Python-declared `Stat` and `Chart` does. There is
one aggregation engine in this package; a card built in the UI is not a second,
lesser one.

A card may also carry a **filter**, re-expressed as the query string the list page's
own filter rail would produce — the same parsing, the same rejection of a parameter
the panel does not own. A filter path that would fan rows out through a to-many join is
refused outright rather than silently double-counted: a list page can hide that fan-out
behind `DISTINCT`, but a sum cannot, and a card reporting a number nobody can reproduce
is worse than a card that refuses to build.

**The model picker only ever offers what the viewer may already open** —
`permissions.visible_panels(request, ...)`, computed before any cap is applied, because
capping a registry slice *before* filtering it by permission is exactly the bug that
once gave a restricted user a blank default dashboard (see
[the default dashboard](#the-default-dashboard)). Every field offered for aggregation,
grouping or dating is drawn from that model's own panel, so the picker can never offer
a column the panel does not expose, and the same allowlist validates the POST that
follows — the editor cannot offer a control whose value the write end would then
reject.

### Rearranging, hiding, and the two save scopes

Cards drag to reorder within the grid and resize across it (1 to 4 columns wide); a
declared card can be switched off (`show: False`) without touching the Python that
declares it, and a UI-built card can be deleted outright.

Saving for yourself is the default. Saving "for everyone" — what every colleague sees
tomorrow morning — needs the same permission [the customisation rail's site-wide
save](lists.md#the-customisation-rail) does,
[`LIST_PREFS_PERMISSION`](settings.md#behaviour) (superuser by default): a request for
the site-wide row without it is refused outright rather than quietly downgraded to a
personal save, because a silent downgrade looks exactly like success and the person
would never learn their colleagues saw nothing change. "Reset" writes `NULL`, not
today's resolved layout, for the same reason a Python `panel.py` has to stay the
answer after a reset — see [How configuration resolves](configuration.md).

### `known_keys`: telling "removed" from "not yet seen"

A declared card the stored arrangement never mentions is appended at the end rather
than dropped — the same choice `NAV_UNLISTED = "append"` makes for the sidebar, and for
the same reason: a developer adding a card to `get_widgets()` after a colleague last
saved an arrangement must not have it silently swallowed by that older row.

But "never mentions" is ambiguous by itself — a key absent from a stored arrangement is
either a card that did not exist when the arrangement was last saved, or one that did
and was deliberately left out. `known_keys` is the snapshot that tells the two apart:
every declared key that existed in the code the moment the layout was last written is
recorded on the row alongside it. A key recorded there and now absent from the
arrangement was a decision, and stays gone; a key that is neither mentioned nor
recorded is new since that save, and is appended automatically.

```pycon
>>> layout.known_keys      # captured at the moment this row was last saved
['stat:revenue', 'chart:orders-over-time', 'table:latest-orders']
>>> # a fourth card added to get_widgets() afterwards is not in known_keys,
>>> # so it appears on every dashboard using this layout without anyone re-saving
```

### What this costs, and what it does not widen

The two properties that carry the code layer carry this one too: **the permission
check happens before the query**, so a card over a model the viewer cannot see is
neither drawn nor computed and never reaches `aggregate()`; and **the cost is one
aggregate per card**, because every card — declared or UI-built — goes through
`compute_panel` and inherits its join-bucket partitioning rather than growing a second
aggregation path here. A stored arrangement is capped (60 entries total, 24 of them
UI-built — the smaller number bounds the query cost, since a pointer at a declared card
costs nothing the code was not already going to spend) and a card's filter is capped in
length, but neither cap is a security boundary: every card is a validated aggregate
over a column the panel already exposes, never an arbitrary expression.

## The command palette

<kbd>⌘K</kbd> / <kbd>Ctrl+K</kbd>. A palette is a promise that anything reachable by
clicking is reachable by typing, and the only honest way to keep that promise is to
build the list from the same facts the sidebar is built from rather than from a
hand-maintained copy.

So navigation and create commands are derived from the registry and from the registered
pages, every one filtered through the permission layer on the way past. That filtering
is not cosmetic: a palette is *read* as a menu of what you are allowed to do, and
listing "Delete customers" to someone who cannot delete customers is worse than
useless, because they will try.

Commands are shipped to the browser as JSON and filtered there, because a palette that
round-trips on every keystroke of "das" to find "Dashboard" is not a palette. Record
search is the opposite case and goes to the server.

Add your own:

```python
site.register_command(
    id="reindex-search",
    label="Reindex search",
    url="/ops/reindex/",
    icon="refresh-cw",
    section="Actions",
    permission="ops.run_reindex",
)
```

`id` is required — it is what lets a plugin replace a command a project registered first
(or vice versa) instead of the palette silently carrying two rows for the same action.

Switch the whole thing off with `VANTAGE["COMMAND_PALETTE"] = False`. The global search
results page stays available and styled either way.

## See also

- [Analytics](analytics.md) — `Stat` and `Chart` in full
- [Permissions](permissions.md) — how a widget is gated
- [Extending](extending.md) — slots, for putting your own HTML on an existing page
- [Settings](settings.md) — `DASHBOARD`, `COMMAND_PALETTE`
- [How configuration resolves](configuration.md) — the resolution order the dashboard's
  UI arrangement layer follows, stated once for every surface that uses it
- [Lists](lists.md#the-customisation-rail) — the same UI-override pattern, one page
  over, including `LIST_PREFS_PERMISSION` and what "reset" actually does to the row

# Theming

[← Index](index.md)

One colour drives the whole palette. Everything else is derived from it, in both
themes, with the contrast checked numerically rather than by eye.

```python
# settings.py
VANTAGE = {
    "SITE_TITLE":  "Acme",
    "SITE_ACRONYM": "AC",
    "LOGO":        "img/acme.svg",
    "LOGO_DARK":   "img/acme-light.svg",
    "FAVICON":     "img/favicon.png",
    "BRAND_COLOR": "#0ea5e9",
    "BRAND_RADIUS": "0.5rem",
    "THEME":       "system",
}
```

Every one of those can also be changed **inside the panel** by a superuser, without a
deploy. See [the settings screen](#the-settings-screen).

## `BRAND_COLOR` and the derived palette

Supplying one colour and expecting the panel to look like yours means more than tinting
a button. Every interactive surface needs a matching hover, a focus ring, a subtle
accent, and — the part usually got wrong — a foreground colour that is actually
readable on top of it, in both themes, for *any* hue you might pick.

### Why OKLCH

Working in OKLCH is what makes this tractable. It is perceptually uniform, so holding
lightness constant while changing hue produces colours that genuinely look equally
light, which sRGB emphatically does not. That lets the derivation pick lightness
*targets* per role and per theme and trust them across the hue circle.

The whole conversion chain — sRGB transfer function, OKLab matrices, gamut clamping,
WCAG contrast — is implemented in `vantage.color` with no dependencies.

### What is derived

Six tokens per theme:

| Token | |
|---|---|
| `--primary` | the brand surface: buttons, active states, chart fills |
| `--primary-foreground` | text on top of it, guaranteed to clear WCAG AA |
| `--primary-hover` | moved away from the page background: darker on light, lighter on dark |
| `--ring` | the focus ring |
| `--accent` | a heavily desaturated tint, for selected rows and subtle fills |
| `--accent-foreground` | text on the accent |

Only these vary with `BRAND_COLOR`. **The neutral greys are fixed**, and that split
matters: a site owner supplying one colour should get a branded panel, not a panel where
their colour has leaked into the page background and the table borders.

### The contrast guarantee

The derived primary and its foreground clear **WCAG AA at 4.5:1 for every input hue**.
The tests sweep the hue circle to prove it.

The mechanism: aim the primary at a lightness target (0.55 on light, 0.70 on dark),
pick whichever of near-white or near-black reads better on it, and if that pair is
still below 4.5:1, walk the lightness away from the target in both directions and take
whichever reaches AA with the **smaller** move.

Some hues — saturated yellows especially — cannot hold text at a mid lightness,
so the primary has to move. Moving it is the correct failure mode; shipping an
unreadable button is not.

Measured:

```pycon
>>> derive_palette("#0ea5e9")            # light theme
{'primary': 'oklch(0.5500 0.1208 237.32)',
 'primary-foreground': 'oklch(0.9850 0.0072 237.32)', ...}
# contrast 4.57 : 1

>>> derive_palette("#facc15")            # a saturated yellow, light theme
# primary oklch(0.5500 0.1126 91.94), foreground oklch(0.9850 …) — contrast 4.66 : 1

>>> derive_palette("#0d9488")            # teal; the target had to move
# primary oklch(0.5400 …) rather than 0.5500 — contrast 4.62 : 1

>>> derive_palette("#0ea5e9", dark=True)
# primary oklch(0.7000 0.1479 237.32), foreground oklch(0.1600 …) — contrast 7.41 : 1
```

Two details in the small print. The foreground is **not** pure white or black: a hint of
the brand hue keeps the pairing from looking like an unstyled default and costs almost
nothing in contrast. And gamut clamping gives up **chroma** while holding lightness and
hue, because a slightly duller colour still reads as the brand whereas a shifted
lightness breaks the very guarantee this exists to provide.

## Tokens

The token contract is shadcn/ui's, because it is well designed and widely understood: a
small set of semantic **role** names rather than a palette of colour names. No component
ever hard-codes a colour, so the whole appearance is controlled from one place.

Twenty-seven tokens per theme — twenty-one fixed neutrals plus the six derived above:

```
background            foreground
card                  card-foreground
popover               popover-foreground
primary               primary-foreground     primary-hover
secondary             secondary-foreground
muted                 muted-foreground
accent                accent-foreground
destructive           destructive-foreground
success               success-foreground
warning               warning-foreground
border   input   ring
sidebar  sidebar-foreground  sidebar-border
```

Plus `--radius`, from `BRAND_RADIUS`.

The neutrals are very slightly cool rather than pure grey, which is what stops a panel
looking like an unstyled document. The dark background is a near-black with a trace of
the same cool hue rather than `#000`, which keeps elevation readable and avoids the
smeary look on OLED.

## Light, dark and system

`VANTAGE["THEME"]` is `"light"`, `"dark"` or `"system"` (the default).

Both themes are **always emitted**, in this order:

```css
:root { --radius: 0.5rem; --background: oklch(1 0 0); ... }        /* light */

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { ... }                          /* system */
}

:root[data-theme="dark"] { ... }                                   /* explicit */
```

Light lives on **bare `:root`**, so a page with no theme information still renders
correctly. Dark is applied under both an explicit `data-theme="dark"` and a
`prefers-color-scheme` media query guarded with `:not([data-theme="light"])`.

> Defining a colour only inside a media query is the bug that makes a theme toggle work
> in one direction and not the other.

The stylesheet is **inlined into `<head>`** rather than served as a file, because the
tokens depend on project settings: a static asset would have to be regenerated on every
settings change, and would be wrong for any project running more than one brand.

### No theme flash

A tiny blocking script in `<head>` stamps the saved theme onto `<html>` before first
paint:

```js
(function () {
  try {
    var saved = localStorage.getItem('vantage-theme');
    if (saved === 'dark' || saved === 'light') {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute('data-theme', saved);
    }
  } catch (e) {}
})();
```

It has to be inline and blocking; a deferred script is too late and the page renders
light, then flips.

Server-side, a `vantage-theme` cookie set by the toggle wins over the project default.
The localStorage read covers the very first paint, before any cookie exists. Set
`THEME_TOGGLE = False` to remove the control and pin everyone to `THEME` — including a
user who saved a choice before the toggle was turned off: with it off, neither the
cookie nor the inline script is consulted.

## Right to left

RTL works from day one and needs no configuration. The layout direction comes from
Django's own `get_language_bidi()`, so `<html dir="rtl">` is set whenever the active
language is right-to-left. The stylesheets use logical properties, so nothing needs a
mirrored build.

Set `LANGUAGE_CODE = "ar"` (or use `LocaleMiddleware`) and the panel flips. The
package ships a compiled Arabic catalogue for exactly this — see
[Internationalization](internationalization.md).

## Logos and marks

| Setting | |
|---|---|
| `LOGO` | Shown in the sidebar |
| `LOGO_DARK` | Swapped in for the dark theme — when it is pinned, and when the device prefers dark and nothing is pinned. Falls back to `LOGO` when unset |
| `FAVICON` | The browser tab icon |
| `SITE_ACRONYM` | Two letters for the collapsed sidebar, shown there even when a `LOGO` is set (a wide logo has no room); derived from `SITE_TITLE` when unset |

Each accepts a static path (`"img/acme.svg"`), resolved with `{% static %}`, or an
already-resolved URL — `/…`, `//…`, `http://…`, `https://…` or a `data:` URI — which
passes through untouched. That second case is what makes an uploaded logo work:
`{% static %}` would mangle `/media/vantage/logo.svg` into
`/static/media/vantage/logo.svg`.

`SITE_ACRONYM` takes the first letter of each of the first two words —
`"Acme Corporation"` → `AC` — or the first two characters of a single-word title.

## Custom CSS

```python
VANTAGE = {"CUSTOM_CSS": "css/admin-overrides.css"}
```

A stylesheet loaded after Vantage's own, so it can override anything. Because every
component reads tokens, the most useful thing to put in it is usually a token
redefinition rather than a component rule:

```css
:root {
  --radius: 0;
  --sidebar: oklch(0.98 0.01 250);
}

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:not([data-theme="light"]) {
    --sidebar: oklch(0.15 0.01 250);
  }
}

:root[data-theme="dark"] {
  --sidebar: oklch(0.15 0.01 250);
}
```

Define a token in all three places — bare `:root`, the media query and the explicit
`[data-theme="dark"]` selector — or the toggle will work in one direction only.

`CUSTOM_CSS` is deliberately **not** editable from the settings screen. It is code, not
configuration.

## The settings screen

`/admin/_/settings/`. A superuser can change the branding, appearance and behaviour of
the panel without a deploy, and the stored value sits **underneath** the file settings:

```
SiteConfiguration row  >  settings.VANTAGE  >  conf.DEFAULTS
```

Three sections:

| Section | Fields |
|---|---|
| Branding | site title, short mark, logo, dark logo, favicon, login image |
| Appearance | brand colour, corner radius, default theme, theme toggle |
| Behaviour | environment banner, rows per page, command palette, read-only mode |

One **Save** stores the whole form. Each section has its own **Reset**, which acts on
exactly the fields that card shows, so a button can never clear something it does not
display. A fourth card, **Sidebar**, arranges the navigation: rename, re-icon, reorder
and regroup items, hide them, add groups and links. Its Reset hands the sidebar back to
whatever `panel.py` and `VANTAGE["NAV"]` declare.

### What it deliberately cannot change

An explicit allowlist, not "every key with a matching column", because the line it
draws is a security boundary and it should be readable in one screenful.

Absent on purpose: `AUTO_REGISTER`, `EXCLUDE`, `INCLUDE_ONLY`, `NAV`, `NAV_UNLISTED`,
`DASHBOARD`, `PERMISSIONS`, `SETTINGS_PERMISSION`, `LIST_PREFS_PERMISSION`,
`AUDIT_LOG`, `CUSTOM_CSS`, `IMPORT_MAX_BYTES`, `IMPORT_MAX_ROWS`. Those are code, not
configuration: they decide what exists and who may reach it.

`SETTINGS_PERMISSION` in particular is never editable from the UI — that would be a
self-grant.

### Who may open it

Superusers, unless `VANTAGE["SETTINGS_PERMISSION"]` widens it. Superuser-only is the
honest default: this screen can rebrand the site, switch the panel to read-only, and
upload a file that every other user's browser will load.

```python
VANTAGE = {
    # a permission string...
    "SETTINGS_PERMISSION": "vantage.change_siteconfiguration",
    # ...or a callable taking the request
    # "SETTINGS_PERMISSION": lambda request: request.user.groups.filter(name="ops").exists(),
}
```

### Three things the screen does that a generic model form cannot

**Show what "empty" means.** Every control displays the value it falls back to when
cleared, because "clear this field" is only a safe instruction if you can see where it
lands. That value is the cascade with the database taken out of it.

**Preview the brand colour honestly.** The preview is rendered by the same colour code
that will render the panel — fetched from the view rather than reimplemented in
JavaScript, because two implementations of a colour space is two answers to the same
question.

**Say when the colour was adjusted.** Silently shipping a different colour from the one
that was typed is the kind of thing that gets blamed on the browser for a week. When the
derivation had to move the lightness, the screen says so:

> `#facc15` cannot carry readable text at the lightness this panel uses for buttons: it
> scores 3.1:1 against the text colour that would sit on it, and WCAG AA needs 4.5:1.
> The derived button colour was darkened until it reached 4.7:1. Your colour is stored
> exactly as you entered it.

### Uploads are treated as hostile

`FileField` rather than `ImageField`, because Pillow is not a dependency and never will
be for this — which means the validation Pillow would have done has to be written out.

- Extensions: `.svg`, `.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.webp`. Nothing else.
- Size: 2 MiB. A logo is a logo; anything larger is a mistake or an attempt to fill a
  disk.
- **SVGs are scanned and refused**, not sanitised. An SVG is served from the panel's own
  origin, so a `<script>` inside one runs with the session cookie of whoever views the
  page — and the logo is on every screen, so that is everyone. Refused constructs:
  `<script>`, inline `on…` handlers, an animation that writes an event handler,
  `javascript:` URLs, and embedded documents (`<foreignObject>`, `<iframe>`, `<embed>`,
  `<object>`).

  A rejection filter rather than a rewriter, because a rewriter that is wrong once is
  worse than a refusal that is occasionally annoying. Serving media from a separate
  origin remains the defence in depth this cannot replace.

- Validation runs **on the field**, not only in the form, so a shell session or a data
  migration cannot route around it.

`BRAND_RADIUS` is validated as a CSS length (`0`, `0.5rem`, `8px`, `50%`) because it is
interpolated straight into a `<style>` block, and is therefore not free text.

## The environment banner

```python
VANTAGE = {"ENVIRONMENT": "Staging — data here is not real"}
```

A strip across the top of every page. Setting it to an empty string from the settings
screen hides a banner that `settings.py` asked for, which is exactly why every stored
column is nullable and `NULL` means "not overridden" — a blank value is a legitimate
override.

## See also

- [Settings](settings.md) — every key, with defaults
- [Accessibility](accessibility.md) — the contrast guarantee in its wider context
- [Analytics](analytics.md#charts) — charts follow `--primary` and `currentColor`
- [Deployment](deployment.md#static-files) — serving the CSS
