# UI theme presets

`THEME` decides light or dark. A **UI theme** decides the *look*: the greys, the corners,
the shadows. Vantage ships ten, in the spirit of shadcn/ui's themes, and the default is
the look it has always had.

![The look picker on the account page](assets/screenshots/themes-light.webp){ .dv-shot .dv-only-light }
![The look picker on the account page](assets/screenshots/themes-dark.webp){ .dv-shot .dv-only-dark }

```python
VANTAGE = {
    "UI_THEME": "shadcn",      # the site default; "vantage" if you say nothing
}
```

| Preset | Neutrals | Primary | Corners |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `vantage` | cool zinc | your `BRAND_COLOR` | `0.5rem` |
| `shadcn` | achromatic | near-black (near-white in dark) | `0.625rem`, flat shadows |
| `slate`, `stone`, `zinc` | blue-grey, warm grey, cool grey | near-black / near-white | `0.625rem` |
| `rose`, `blue`, `green`, `violet`, `orange` | achromatic | the accent hue | `0.625rem` |

`vantage` is byte-identical to the stylesheet earlier releases emitted; a regression test
holds it there.

## Your brand colour still wins

A preset's primary is a *default*. If you set `BRAND_COLOR` (in `VANTAGE` or on the
settings screen) every preset derives its buttons, links and focus rings from it, and
only the neutrals, radius and shadows change. The same goes for an explicit
`BRAND_RADIUS`. "Set" means set: choosing `#6366f1` on purpose still counts.

## Letting people choose

```python
VANTAGE = {"UI_THEME_TOGGLE": True}   # the default
```

With it on, **Your account** shows a card per preset. Clicking one repaints the page at
once (the preset's tokens are fetched from `_/ui-theme/<name>.css` and swapped in) and
stores the choice in a cookie, which the server reads, so the next page arrives already
in that look. There is no flash because there is nothing for a script to correct. Set it
to `False` to pin everyone to `UI_THEME`; the site default can also be changed from the
settings screen.

Only the active preset's tokens are in a page, so choosing a preset costs nothing extra.

## Your own presets

```python
VANTAGE = {
    "UI_THEME": "paper",
    "UI_THEMES": {
        "paper": {
            "label": "Paper",
            "light": {"background": "oklch(0.98 0.012 90)", "border": "oklch(0.88 0.02 90)"},
            "dark": {"background": "oklch(0.2 0.01 60)"},
            "primary": "#0d9488",          # used only while BRAND_COLOR is unset
            "radius": "0.25rem",
            "shadows": {"sm": "none", "md": "none", "lg": "0 2px 8px oklch(0 0 0 / 0.15)"},
            "border_width": "1px",
            "font": "Georgia, serif",
            "extras": {"sidebar-width": "17rem"},
        }
    },
}
```

Everything is optional; **what you leave out is inherited from `vantage`**. Keys are
checked when settings load, with a did-you-mean (`"raduis"` suggests `"radius"`; so does a
misspelt token). A custom name that matches a built-in replaces it.

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `light`, `dark` | Neutral tokens: `background`, `foreground`, `card`, `muted`, `muted-foreground`, `border`, `input`, `sidebar`, `destructive`, `success`, `warning`, ... |
| `primary` | Hex colour the brand tokens are derived from, when `BRAND_COLOR` is unset |
| `light_brand`, `dark_brand` | Brand tokens set outright (`primary`, `primary-foreground`, `primary-hover`, `ring`, `accent`, `accent-foreground`) instead of derived |
| `radius` | `--radius` |
| `shadows` | `sm`, `md`, `lg` box-shadow values |
| `border_width` | Width of card and panel borders |
| `font` | `--font-sans` |
| `extras` | Any other custom property, without the leading `--` |

### Keep it legible

Presets are tested, light and dark, for the pairs a reader depends on: text on its
surface (4.5:1), muted text on the page, cards and muted fills, button text on the
primary, and the form-field border against every surface (3:1). Run the same checks on
your own preset with `vantage.theme.build_tokens(preset="paper", dark=True)` and
`vantage.color.contrast_ratio`; see `tests/test_presets.py`.

The standalone 500 page copies the `vantage` neutrals on purpose (it must render when
nothing else can) and does not follow presets.

---

URL: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/django-vantage/phones/

# Phones

Below `40rem` (640px) the panel switches to a phone layout. There is nothing to turn on
and no second template: it is the same markup, restacked by one stylesheet
(`vantage-mobile.css`) that is linked with a media query, so a desktop never loads it
and looks exactly as before.

![Orders as cards on a phone](assets/screenshots/phone-orders-light.webp){ .dv-shot .dv-only-light }
![Orders as cards on a phone](assets/screenshots/phone-orders-dark.webp){ .dv-shot .dv-only-dark }

| On a phone | Instead of |
| --- | --- |
| Each row is a **card**: a title, a few label/value pairs, and a checkbox | a table you scroll sideways |
| Bulk actions open in a **bottom sheet** when something is selected | a bar above the table |
| Navigation is a **drawer** behind the menu button | a sidebar |
| The filter rail starts **folded** | an open rail ahead of the first record |
| The header search shrinks to its icon and still opens the palette | a search box |
| Detail and form pages are one column | two |

It follows every UI theme preset and dark mode, because it uses the same colour,
radius and shadow tokens as everything else.

## Which fields a card shows

By default a card shows the first column as its title and the next three as labelled
values. To choose, name the columns in `card_fields` — the same line the gallery and the
board read for the cards under their titles:

```python
@register(Order)
class OrderPanel(ModelPanel):
    list_display = ["number", "status", "customer", "total", "created_at"]
    card_fields = ["total", "status"]     # a phone card: number, then these two
```

The first column is always the title. A name that is not in `list_display` is ignored: a
card is the table's own row restacked, not a second renderer, so it can only show what
the table has. Sorting stays available, as a strip of buttons above the cards.

## The bottom sheet

![The bulk-action sheet with two reviews selected](assets/screenshots/phone-sheet-light.webp){ .dv-shot .dv-only-light }
![The bulk-action sheet with two reviews selected](assets/screenshots/phone-sheet-dark.webp){ .dv-shot .dv-only-dark }

Ticking a card opens the sheet along the bottom edge, with the count, the same actions
as the desktop bar, and **Clear selection**. It is a non-modal dialog, on purpose: the
checkboxes behind it are still being ticked, so focus is neither moved into it when it
opens nor trapped inside it. **Escape** or **Clear selection** closes it, clears the
selection and puts focus back on the last card you touched. The count is announced as it
changes, as on the desktop, and the sheet only carries `role="dialog"` while it is a
sheet.

## Touch targets, zoom and the notch

- Buttons, inputs, selects, the card checkbox and navigation links are at least 44px
  tall.
- Fields are at least 16px, so iOS Safari does not zoom the page when one is focused.
- The page never scrolls sideways. A wide table elsewhere still scrolls inside its own
  box.
- The shell asks for `viewport-fit=cover` and pads the header, content, sheet, save bar
  and toasts by `env(safe-area-inset-*)`, so nothing sits under a notch or the home
  indicator.
- The sheet and the drawer slide in unless `prefers-reduced-motion` is set, in which
  case they appear.

## Limits

- The breakpoint is the width of the screen, not the device. A phone held sideways is
  wider than `40rem` and gets the tablet layout (the table, with the drawer for
  navigation).
- The table's resize, pin and column-visibility controls have no meaning on a card and
  are hidden. The totals strip under the table is hidden too.
- The board, calendar, gallery and map views are unchanged; they already scroll inside
  their own boxes.
- The inline-edit changeset bar keeps its desktop design, wrapped and padded for the safe area.

---

URL: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/django-vantage/permissions/

# Permissions

[← Index](index.md)

Every access decision in the panel goes through one object. There is no second place
where a view decides for itself whether you may do something, and that is the point: a
guard in the views has to be remembered on every new write path, and the one that gets
forgotten is the one that matters.

## The three layers

Three concerns that look alike and must not be conflated.

| Layer | Question | Called | Method |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Model** | May this user see this section at all? | once per page | `has_model_perm(request, model, action)` |
| **Object** | May this user act on *this* row? | only where N is 1 | `has_object_perm(request, model, action, obj)` |
| **Queryset** | Which rows may this user see? | once per query | `filter_queryset(request, queryset, action)` |

Keeping them apart is not tidiness. It is the difference between a list page that runs
two queries and one that runs a hundred.

The four actions are `view`, `add`, `change` and `delete`, mapped to Django's codenames
through `get_permission_codename` — never an f-string on `model_name`, because the
helper respects proxy models and a custom `Meta.model_name`.

```pycon
>>> PanelPermissions().perm_name(Order, "change")
'shop.change_order'
```

## Why `filter_queryset` must be bulk

This is the single most important thing on the page.

Django's `ModelBackend` returns an **empty permission set whenever `obj is not None`**,
*and* only populates its permission cache when `obj is None`. So calling
`has_perm(perm, obj)` once per row on a hundred-row page executes a hundred uncached
queries under django-guardian. That is the most common performance failure in
object-permission admin UIs.

So: **override `filter_queryset`, never a loop over `has_object_perm`.**

```python
from vantage.permissions import PanelPermissions


class OwnerScopedPermissions(PanelPermissions):
    def filter_queryset(self, request, queryset, action="view"):
        if hasattr(queryset.model, "owner"):
            return queryset.filter(owner=request.user)
        return queryset
```

```pycon
>>> Order.objects.count()
200
>>> permissions.filter_queryset(request, Order.objects.all()).count()
37
```

> If what you actually want is **multi-tenancy** — every model scoped to the signed-in
> user's organisation, with fail-closed checks that name every model tenancy cannot
> place — do not hand-roll it the way the example above does. `hasattr(model,
> "tenant")` guesses at which field is the tenant column and says nothing when it
> guesses wrong; [`vantage.tenancy`](tenancy.md) is the real subsystem this package
> ships for exactly that job, with resolvers for the common ways a tenant is
> identified (a user attribute, a subdomain, a trusted header), and it composes onto
> this same `filter_queryset` seam automatically once `VANTAGE["TENANT_MODEL"]` is set.
> The pattern above is still the right shape for row scoping that is not
> tenancy — "only your own orders", say.

The base implementation does no row filtering at all: model-level permissions have
already gated entry, which is exactly Django's own model. Because it is a no-op by
default, the call costs nothing until a project overrides it — which is why every call
site can make it unconditionally, and does:

- the list page, before filters and search;
- the detail, edit and delete pages, before the object is fetched;
- the exporter and the importer;
- global search and the relation autocomplete;
- dashboard widgets, so a number computed over rows you cannot list is not a leak;
- saved views, on every request, which is why a shared view can never widen access.

### Alternatively, `get_queryset`

For scoping that belongs to one model rather than to the whole panel, override
`get_queryset` on the panel:

```python
@register(Invoice)
class InvoicePanel(ModelPanel):
    def get_queryset(self, request):
        return super().get_queryset(request).filter(owner=request.user)
```

`get_queryset` is the base for **every** view of that model. `filter_queryset` is the
policy applied to every model. Use whichever matches the shape of your rule; they
compose.

## The resolution order

`has_model_perm` answers in this order, and the order is deliberate:

1. **Not authenticated** → no.
2. **[Read-only mode](#read-only-mode) and this is a write** → no. Before the superuser
   bypass, because read-only is an operational choice about the deployment, not about
   who is asking.
3. **The panel's own `has_<action>_permission` hook**, if it has one. Returning `None`
   means "no opinion".
4. **Superuser** → yes.
5. `user.has_perm("app.action_model")`.

`has_object_perm` runs the same sequence with the object passed through, and then
short-circuits to the model-level answer if **no configured backend can actually answer
an object-level question**. `ModelBackend` demonstrably cannot; if it is the only
backend, object checks are dead weight and walking the chain per row is pointless.

```pycon
>>> PanelPermissions().supports_object_permissions
False                     # only ModelBackend is installed
```

## Per-panel hooks

Define any of these on a `ModelPanel` and it is consulted **before the superuser
bypass**:

```python
@register(Invoice)
class InvoicePanel(ModelPanel):
    def has_delete_permission(self, request, obj=None):
        return False
```

```pycon
>>> permissions.has_model_perm(request_as_superuser, Invoice, "delete")
False
>>> permissions.has_model_perm(request_as_superuser, Order, "delete")   # no hook
True
```

A panel that says nobody may delete these rows means **nobody**. Adopting an
`admin.py` into Vantage must not quietly widen a refusal to every superuser.

The signature is `(request, obj=None)` for all four verbs, including `add` —
`contrib.admin` omits `obj` on that one alone, and one uniform signature is worth more
than bug-compatibility with an inconsistency. The
[`contrib.admin` adapter](extending.md) bridges the difference so an adopted
`has_add_permission(self, request)` still works.

Do **not** put row scoping in these hooks. They are the N-is-1 layer.

## Superusers

`superuser_bypass = True` by default. Django's own admin does the same, and a panel that
can lock out the superuser is a support burden rather than a security feature.

Two things sit above the bypass and are not negotiable by it: read-only mode, and a
panel hook that refuses.

One thing sits *outside* it entirely: **editing somebody else's saved view**. Being able
to rebrand the site is not a reason to be able to rewrite a colleague's private view,
and Save-as is one click away, so a bypass there would buy nothing and cost the only
guarantee the feature makes.

Set `superuser_bypass = False` on your resolver subclass if you need superusers held to
the same permission checks as everyone else.

## Swapping the resolver

```python
# settings.py
VANTAGE = {
    "PERMISSIONS": "myproject.permissions.TenantPermissions",
}
```

A dotted path to a `PanelPermissions` subclass. It is instantiated once and cached; the
cache is dropped when the setting changes, which is what makes `override_settings` work
in tests.

## Third-party backends

Adopted rather than reimplemented. django-guardian and django-rules both work by being
in `AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS`, so `has_perm` already routes to them and both the model
and object layers pick them up with no configuration.

Only the **bulk** path needs an adapter, because `rules` has no queryset story at all
and guardian's lives in a shortcut function.

### django-guardian

```python
VANTAGE = {
    "PERMISSIONS": "vantage.permissions.GuardianPermissions",
}
```

That is the only supported bulk adapter, because guardian is the only one of the two
with a bulk API. It narrows every queryset with `get_objects_for_user`, and:

- `accept_global_perms=True` — a model-level grant should still mean "all rows", or
  granting someone blanket access would paradoxically show them nothing;
- `with_superuser=True`;
- an anonymous or unauthenticated request gets an empty queryset.

It is **not** auto-enabled when guardian is installed. Whether object permissions should
narrow the admin is a policy decision, not a consequence of having the package on the
path.

### django-rules

Add `rules.permissions.ObjectPermissionBackend` to `AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS` and your
predicates apply at the model and object layers automatically —
`supports_object_permissions` becomes true, and per-row checks start routing to your
rules.

`rules` has no way to express "which rows", so it cannot scope a list page on its own.
Write the queryset half yourself:

```python
class RulesPermissions(PanelPermissions):
    def filter_queryset(self, request, queryset, action="view"):
        if queryset.model is Project:
            return queryset.filter(members=request.user)
        return queryset
```

## Read-only mode

```python
VANTAGE = {"READ_ONLY": True}
```

or, better, with a reason:

```python
VANTAGE = {"READ_ONLY": "Frozen during the migration window."}
```

A string doubles as the explanation shown to the user, which beats a bare "permission
denied" for something that is a deliberate operational choice.

**It is enforced in the permission layer, not in the views.** Denying the permission
means every existing check — buttons, actions, forms (including
[editable inlines](forms.md#editable-inlines), which submit as part of the parent
form), [inline cell editing](lists.md#inline-cell-editing), the importer,
[duplicate](forms.md#duplicating-a-record) and [bulk edit](forms.md#bulk-edit) —
refuses at once, and a new write path inherits the refusal without anyone thinking
about it.

It refuses exactly `add`, `change` and `delete`. `view` is conspicuously absent.

```pycon
>>> read_only_reason()
'Frozen during the migration window.'
>>> permissions.allowed_actions(request_as_superuser, Order)
{'view'}                                        # superuser, still read-only
>>> client.get("/admin/shop/order/").status_code
200
>>> client.get("/admin/shop/order/add/").status_code
403
```

Superusers are not exempt, deliberately. The whole value of the switch is that it holds
for everyone; an exemption for the account most likely to be signed in during an
incident would make it decorative.

`READ_ONLY` is also editable from the [settings screen](theming.md#the-settings-screen),
so an operator can freeze the panel without a deploy.

### Read-only models and legacy databases

The same refusal, per model. For a panel over tables another system owns — a legacy
database, a reporting replica, a schema Django did not create:

```python
@register(LegacyCustomer)
class LegacyCustomerPanel(ModelPanel):
    read_only = True
    # The exception list: these stay changeable on existing rows. Nothing else does.
    editable_fields = ["notes", "account_manager"]
```

- `read_only = True` refuses `add` and `delete` for everyone, superusers and a panel's
  own `has_*_permission` hooks included, exactly like `READ_ONLY`.
- With `editable_fields` set, `change` stays available (to whoever has the
  permission) and every other field is read-only, through the same field-level layer
  as [field permissions](field-permissions.md) — so forms, inline cell editing, bulk
  edit, the importer and the JSON API all honour it.
- `VANTAGE["UNMANAGED_READ_ONLY"] = True` makes every `Meta.managed = False` model
  read-only unless its panel sets `read_only = False`. It is off by default for
  compatibility; turn it on for a panel pointed at a database Django does not own,
  together with a database user that has only the grants the allowlist needs.

`manage.py check` reports a malformed value (`vantage.E122`) or an allowlist naming
something that is not a field (`vantage.E123`).

## Impersonation

Deliberately narrow: superusers only, never onto another superuser, loud while it is
happening, and recorded. The failure mode being guarded against is someone quietly
acquiring rights they do not have and leaving no trace.

```pycon
>>> can_impersonate(admin)
True
>>> can_impersonate(editor)
False
```

Refusals, each with its own message:

| Attempt | Result |
|---|---|
| Not a superuser | `Only superusers may impersonate.` |
| Yourself | `You are already signed in as that user.` |
| Another superuser | `Superusers cannot be impersonated.` |
| An inactive account | `That account is inactive.` |

Refusing superuser-to-superuser matters: it would be a lateral move that muddies the
audit trail without granting anything useful.

Django's own `login()` machinery is used rather than a request-level user swap, so every
downstream permission check sees the target naturally and **nothing has to know
impersonation exists**. Two session keys track it, written after `login()` because
`login()` flushes the session.

While it is active, a banner across the top of every page says *Acting as X — signed in
as Y*. Loud on purpose: someone acting as another account needs to be unable to forget
it, and anyone looking over their shoulder needs to see it too. Both the start and the
end are logged at `warning` level to the `vantage.security` logger with both usernames
and both ids.

`real_user(request)` returns the account actually signed in, whoever is being
impersonated.

## The audit log

`VANTAGE["AUDIT_LOG"]` is on by default. It records **what a person did through this
admin** — one row per create, edit, delete or bulk action, with the actor.

That is a much smaller thing than row history, and the difference is why
django-simple-history is soft-detected rather than required: it creates a history model
*in your own app*, which means a migration in your code and roughly double the write
volume on every table it touches. Making that the price of installing an admin panel is
not a trade a panel gets to make for you. When you have chosen it, its timeline renders
next to Vantage's own.

Three rules follow from the scope.

**Never a `post_save` signal.** A receiver cannot see who was logged in — the actor is
the single most valuable column in the table. It would also faithfully log the nightly
import job and every `shell` session, which is the row history we just declined to
build, minus the actor, at the same cost. Entries are written from the two places a
person's intent is actually known: the form views and the bulk-action runner.

**The diff never carries a secret and never carries a file.** Field names are matched
against the same [`SENSITIVE` pattern](inference.md#the-sensitive-name-exclusion) that
keeps a password column out of a list page — imported rather than restated, so the two
can never drift apart — and a file field records the *name* it was given, never a byte
of its contents. An audit log is read by more people than the records it describes.

**Logging never breaks the write it describes.** Every entry goes through a writer that
catches everything, logs it and returns `None`, and it is called *outside* the
transaction that performed the write.

The log has its own page and its own gate, which is stricter than a model permission:
the log spans every model in the panel, so someone who may not see orders can still
learn a great deal from a list of who has been editing them. It is deliberately not a
registered panel — a generic list page over it would come with an Add button, an edit
form and a delete action, and an audit log you can edit is not an audit log.

Each record's [History](history.md) page replays its entries to show the record as it
was at any earlier point, and restores fields from there.

## Panels a user cannot see

Never rendered. `visible_panels` filters the sidebar, the command palette, global
search, the schema map and the default dashboard through `has_model_perm`.

```pycon
>>> len(permissions.visible_panels(request_as_admin, list(site.panels())))
9
>>> len(permissions.visible_panels(request_as_plain_staff, list(site.panels())))
0
```

Two details worth stating.

**A declared `NAV` can reorder, rename and hide — it can never grant access.** Every
entry still passes through the permission layer, so a nav entry for a model you cannot
open does not render.

**The default dashboard filters by permission *before* capping.** Capping first would
mean a user who can see only one model, and whose model sorts outside the first twelve,
gets an entirely empty dashboard — the cap would silently have become an access rule.

**A dashboard widget is gated before it is computed**, not after. A card that computes a
number and then hides it has already leaked it into the query log and paid for it.

## A row you may not see does not exist

Every object lookup goes through `filter_queryset` before any object-level check runs,
so an out-of-scope record answers **404**, not 403. Answering 403 would confirm that
record 12 exists and is merely off-limits, which is the leak the scoping was for.

Once the row is known to be in scope, an object-level refusal *is* a 403 — by that point
you already know the record is there.

The same reasoning shapes two other refusals:

- A bulk action you may not run and a bulk action that no longer exists both answer
  "that action is not available". Nothing happens, and we do not say which it was.
- The autocomplete endpoint answers `Unknown model.` for a model that is not registered
  and for one you cannot view, so it cannot be used to probe what exists.

## Sign-in

Every panel view requires an authenticated user with `is_staff`. Anonymous visitors are
redirected to `settings.LOGIN_URL` with a `next` parameter. Vantage ships styled
sign-in, sign-out and change-password views over `django.contrib.auth`'s own forms —
mount them, or keep your own. See
[Signing in](getting-started.md#signing-in).

## See also

- [Multi-tenancy](tenancy.md) — row scoping by tenant, built on `filter_queryset`
- [How configuration resolves](configuration.md) — why permissions and tenancy stay
  Python-only while other things gained a UI layer
- [Settings](settings.md#behaviour) — `PERMISSIONS`, `READ_ONLY`, `SETTINGS_PERMISSION`, `LIST_PREFS_PERMISSION`, `AUDIT_LOG`
- [Panels](panels.md#permission-hooks) — the per-panel hooks
- [Security](security.md) — login throttling, security headers, and the `--deploy` checks
- [Deployment](deployment.md) — what to switch on before going live

---

URL: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/django-vantage/roles/

# Roles & permissions

Vantage ships a built-in screen for Django's `auth.Group`, treated as what every project
uses it for: a **role**, a named bundle of permissions you grant to people. It lives at
`<panel>/_/roles/`, appears under **System** in the sidebar and in the ⌘K palette, and
needs no configuration. Model permissions live in the tables `django.contrib.auth`
already has; the one table of Vantage's own holds [field permissions](field-permissions.md).

![The permission matrix for one role](assets/screenshots/role-matrix-light.webp){ .dv-shot .dv-only-light }
![The permission matrix for one role](assets/screenshots/role-matrix-dark.webp){ .dv-shot .dv-only-dark }

## What it does

- **Roles list** — every role with its member and permission counts. Create, duplicate
  (permissions and field rules are copied, members are not), rename and delete.
- **Permission matrix** — one row per model, grouped by app; columns for the four
  standard verbs (*view*, *add*, *change*, *delete*) plus an **Other** column holding any
  custom permissions (`Meta.permissions`). Tri-state checkboxes toggle a whole row, a
  whole column, a whole app, or everything shown. Sections fold, and a filter box narrows
  rows by model name, app or codename.
- **Field access** — a **Fields** column on every model this panel shows makes single
  fields *hidden* or *read-only* for the role. Changes join the same pending diff and
  review dialog. See [Field permissions](field-permissions.md).
- **Pending diff and review** — the toolbar counts what you have changed (`+12 / −3`) and
  marks each changed cell. *Review & save* opens a dialog listing every grant and revoke;
  confirming sends **one POST** that is applied in one transaction, or not at all.
- **Members** — add people with a searchable picker (the same combobox as every relation
  field) and remove them. Each member links to their **effective permissions**: the union
  of every role and their direct grants, with the source of each permission shown, and
  the fields their roles hide or make read-only.
- **Delete preview** — before a role is deleted, the page says how many people would lose
  access, counted *net* of every other role and direct grant they hold.

Models this panel does not register — framework tables, excluded models, content types
whose model has been removed — are still listed, in a final **Other models** section,
because those permissions are real and a role can hold them. The *Hide models not in this
panel* toggle hides that section; the choice is remembered per browser.

## Who can use it

Superusers only, by default. Widen it with `ROLES_PERMISSION`, which takes a permission
string or a callable receiving the request — the same shape as `SETTINGS_PERMISSION`:

```python
VANTAGE = {
    "ROLES_PERMISSION": "auth.change_group",
    # or: lambda request: request.user.groups.filter(name="IT").exists()
}
```

Getting in is not the same as being able to change things. Each write also asks the
[permission layer](permissions.md) for the matching verb on `auth.Group` — `add` to
create or duplicate, `change` to edit the matrix, rename or change members, `delete` to
delete — so [read-only mode](permissions.md#read-only-mode) turns the screen into a
viewer, exactly as it does every other screen.

To switch the screen off for everyone, `"ROLES_PERMISSION": lambda request: False`: it
leaves the sidebar and the palette, and every route answers 403.

### Nobody can grant what they do not hold

Widening access is safe because of one rule, enforced on the server for every request:
someone who is not a superuser can only **grant or revoke permissions they hold
themselves** (as `user.get_all_permissions()` reports them, through every authentication
backend). The cells they do not hold render locked, and a forged request that names them
is ignored. Field rules follow the same idea: changing one needs the model's `change`
permission and full access to that field, so nobody can unhide a field hidden from them.

The same rule covers the indirect routes to escalation. Adding a member hands that person
the role's whole bundle — so changing a role's members, renaming it, duplicating it or
deleting it requires holding **every** permission the role grants. "Add myself to Admins"
is refused rather than being a one-click escalation that never touched a checkbox.

Nor can anyone but a superuser change **their own** access. Field rules combine
most-permissively, so joining any role that grants the same model without the rule
would lift it: adding or removing yourself as a member is refused, and so is editing,
renaming or deleting a role you belong to. Someone else has to do it.

A role named in code — in a panel's `field_permissions` or in
`TWO_FACTOR_REQUIRED_ROLES` — cannot be renamed here, because both bind by name and a
rename would silently drop the rule or the requirement for every member.

The screen never shows or edits `is_staff` or `is_superuser`. Only a superuser viewing an
account's effective permissions is told that the account is a superuser.

## Safety properties

- **Every permission id is validated server-side.** Ids are checked against the
  `Permission` table and the actor's reach; unknown, malformed or out-of-reach ids are
  dropped, and the save reports how many were ignored.
- **CSRF on every write** — the views are wrapped in `csrf_protect` themselves, so they
  stay protected even in a project that removed `CsrfViewMiddleware`.
- **Conflicts, not clobbers.** Each page carries a fingerprint of the role's name,
  permission set and field rules. The save compares it *under a write lock* on the group row; if a
  colleague changed the role in the meantime, nothing is saved and the page comes back
  (HTTP 409) showing what they granted and revoked, with your own changes re-applied on
  top for you to review and save again. Rename and delete are checked the same way.
  Membership changes are idempotent additions and removals, so they cannot clobber and
  carry no token.
- **Everything is audited.** Each save writes one [audit log](security.md) entry on the
  role, naming every permission added and removed as `app.codename` and every field rule
  changed as `app.model.field: level`; membership changes
  name the users added and removed; create, rename, duplicate and delete are recorded
  too.

## Performance

The matrix is built from two queries — every `Permission` with its content type, and the
role's permission ids — whatever the number of models — plus one for the role's field
rules. Grouping, verb detection and
"is this model registered here" are worked out in Python against the app registry. The
test suite asserts the page's query count is identical with and without three hundred
extra models. Saving is a constant number of statements however many cells changed.

## Keyboard and screen readers

The matrix is a table of native checkboxes, each named by its permission ("Can change
order"), so Tab and Space work as everywhere else. Arrow keys move between cells like a
spreadsheet (Home/End jump to the ends of a row), section headers are disclosure buttons
with `aria-expanded`, and the tri-state headers expose the *mixed* state. Nothing is
drag-only.

Without JavaScript the page still works: the matrix is a plain form, *Review & save*
submits it directly, and the server works out the diff from the state the page was
rendered with. (A role holding more than Django's `DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_NUMBER_FIELDS`
permissions needs the script, which sends only the changes.)

## Custom user models

Any `AUTH_USER_MODEL` works. Membership is found through the user model's many-to-many to
`Group` (`groups` on `PermissionsMixin`); a user model without one has no members tab, and
the matrix still manages the roles themselves. User search covers whichever of the
username field, email field, `first_name` and `last_name` the model has.

## Reviewing and elevating access

The [access review](access-review.md) lists who can do what across every model, per
person or per role, for audit evidence. [Elevated access](access-review.md#elevated-access-break-glass)
lets someone hold a role for a few minutes with a reason, instead of holding it all year.

---

URL: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/django-vantage/field-permissions/

# Field permissions

[← Index](index.md)

Django's permissions stop at the model: someone who may change an order may change every
column of it. Field permissions add one more level, per [role](roles.md) and per field:

- **Hidden** — the field does not exist for that person. It is not a column, a filter, a
  search path or a sort key; it is not on the detail page, the form, the export or the
  JSON API; it is not in the history or the audit log they read.
- **Read-only** — they see it, everywhere they would see it anyway, and cannot change
  it. Forms render it as text, inline editing skips it, and every write path refuses it
  on the server.

No rule means full access, so nothing changes until you set one. Superusers are never
restricted.

## Setting a rule

### In the roles matrix

Open **System → Roles**, pick a role, and use the **Fields** column next to the model's
permissions. Each model this panel shows has a fold-out list of its fields, each with
*Full access*, *Read-only* or *Hidden*. A changed rule is counted in the toolbar and
marked like a ticked box, and **Review & save** lists it under *Field access* before
anything is written. Permissions and field rules are saved in one transaction, under the
same conflict check: if a colleague changed the role meanwhile, nothing is saved and the
page comes back with their version and your changes re-applied on top.

Rules are stored in the database, one row per role, model and field
(`vantage.FieldPermission`, keyed to `auth.Group`). Deleting a role deletes its rules;
duplicating a role copies them, because they are part of what the role grants.

### In code

One line on the panel:

```python
@register(Order)
class OrderPanel(ModelPanel):
    field_permissions = {"Support": {"total": "readonly", "cost": "hidden"}}
```

Keys are role (group) names. Levels are `"hidden"` and `"readonly"` (`"read-only"` is
accepted too). A role that does not exist is simply never matched. Code rules are added
to whatever the matrix stores; where both name the same field for the same role, the
stricter one applies. The matrix shows a code rule as a *read-only in code* or *hidden in
code* badge — the screen cannot lift it.

A role named here (or in `TWO_FACTOR_REQUIRED_ROLES`) cannot be renamed from the roles
screen: the rule binds by name, so a rename would silently drop it for every member.
Change the code first.

For a rule that depends on the request rather than the role, override
`get_field_access(request)` on the panel and return a `vantage.fieldperms.FieldAccess`.
It only ever adds restrictions, and applies to superusers too:

```python
from vantage.fieldperms import FieldAccess

class OrderPanel(ModelPanel):
    def get_field_access(self, request):
        if request.user.has_perm("shop.close_period"):
            return None
        return FieldAccess(readonly=frozenset({"total"}))
```

`manage.py check` reports a malformed declaration:

| Id | Problem |
|---|---|
| `vantage.E110` | `field_permissions` is not a dict |
| `vantage.E111` | an entry is not `role name → {field: level}` |
| `vantage.E112` | a name is not a field of the model |
| `vantage.E113` | a level is not `"hidden"` or `"readonly"` |
| `vantage.E114` | the rule restricts the primary key, which every link is built from |

## Several roles: most permissive wins

A person in two roles gets the more permissive answer, the same way Django combines
model permissions. If *Support* hides `total` and *Billing* does not, a member of both
sees `total`.

Two refinements stop that from becoming a loophole:

- **Only roles that grant something on the model have a say.** A *Newsletter* role with
  no order permissions says nothing about orders, so it cannot lift Support's rule on
  them. If no role grants the model at all (access came from a direct permission or a
  custom backend), the roles that carry a rule for it are the ones that count.
- **For writing, only roles that grant `add` or `change` on the model have a say.** A
  view-only role that leaves `status` alone shows `status`; it does not combine with a
  change role that made `status` read-only into "may change `status`".

Direct user permissions carry no field rules. The **effective permissions** page for a
person (from a role's *Members* tab) lists what their roles hide and make read-only, per
model, using the same resolution the pages use.

## Where it is enforced

| Surface | Hidden | Read-only |
|---|---|---|
| List columns, phone cards, `card_fields`, related previews | Not a column | Shown |
| Filters, search, `?sort=`, `ordering` | Not offered; refused if named | — |
| Board and calendar "group by", gallery, map | A view arranged by the field is not offered | A board on it cannot be dragged |
| Stat cards, charts, summary bar | A stat or chart that reads it is dropped | Shown |
| Detail page | Not shown | Shown |
| Create, edit and duplicate forms | Not on the page | Text, not an input; a forged value is ignored |
| Child inlines on the edit page | Not a column | Disabled; Django keeps the stored value |
| Inline cell editing | — | Not editable; a forged cell is dropped |
| Bulk edit | Not offered | Not offered; a forged tick writes nothing |
| CSV / TSV / JSON / Excel / PDF export | Not a column | Exported |
| JSON API | Left out of reads, rows and the schema; `?fields=` naming it is a 400 | Writing it is a 400; the schema marks it `readonly` |
| Import | Not a target | Not a target |
| History and restore | Not in the reconstruction or the timeline | Shown, never restorable, refused if posted |
| Audit log, the detail page's history panel | Left out of each diff | Shown |
| Autocomplete and global search | Not searched; a label that prints it becomes `<Model> #<pk>` | — |
| Reveal (sensitive fields) | Refused | — |
| Data quality | Findings about it are dropped | Shown |
| Webhook delivery log | Left out of the body as shown | Shown |
| [Approvals](approvals.md) | Not named or shown; a request touching it cannot be decided by you | Cannot be requested; a request touching it cannot be decided by you |

A create that would need a field the person cannot set — `NOT NULL`, no default — is
refused on the form (and with a 422 from the API) with a sentence saying which field,
rather than failing in the database.

Everything goes through one function, `vantage.fieldperms.access(request, model)`, cached
per request, which asks the permission resolver's `field_access(request, model)`. To
source the rules from somewhere else, override that method on your
[`PanelPermissions`](permissions.md) subclass and return a `FieldAccess(hidden=...,
readonly=...)`. `has_field_perm(request, model, name, "view" | "change")` is there for
your own code.

## With approvals

When a panel also sets [`requires_approval`](approvals.md):

- A **read-only** field is refused, not sent for approval: the person sees "not
  editable" on every path (form, inline, board, API, import, history restore), and no
  change request is made for it.
- A **hidden** field is never named or shown on the approvals queue, the review screen,
  the record's banner or the API. A request touching it shows "1 field you cannot see"
  in its place and leaves out its note and reason. Audit entries for requests read
  `… 1 hidden field (#12)` instead of the field's name.
- **Approving or rejecting a request needs write access to every field in it.** An
  approver for whom one of them is hidden or read-only cannot decide it, and it is not
  counted as waiting for them. A request is applied whole or refused whole, never with
  some fields dropped.

## Webhooks

Webhook payloads are **not** filtered by field permissions. A webhook acts for nobody: it
fires on everyone's changes, and its receiver is chosen by whoever manages webhooks
(superusers and holders of `vantage.manage_webhooks`). Payloads still leave out
[sensitive fields](sensitive-fields.md). Treat `manage_webhooks` as access to every field
of the models a hook subscribes to. The delivery log *page* is read by a person, so it
leaves out the fields hidden from that person.

## What it does not cover

- **Your own code.** A panel method column, a custom template, a `slot` contribution, a
  callable stat or a `save_model` hook that reads a hidden field shows what it reads.
- **`__str__`.** A record label that embeds a hidden value is replaced in autocomplete,
  global search and API records; elsewhere (page titles, foreign-key chips) the label is
  printed as the model returns it. Keep hidden values out of `__str__`.
- **Webhooks**, as above, and anything that reads the database without going through
  the panel: the shell, management commands, `dumpdata`, backups.
- **Superusers**, by design.

---

URL: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/django-vantage/access-review/

# Access review and elevated access

Two tools for the questions an auditor asks about an admin panel: *who can see and
change what*, and *why does anyone hold admin-wide rights all year*.

## Access review

**System → Access review** (also linked from **Roles**) lists, for every active staff
account or for every role:

- which registered models they may **view**, **add**, **change** and **delete**;
- for each field that is **sensitive** or that some role **restricts**: whether they
  can see it, change it and, for a sensitive field, reveal its value.

Superusers are flagged. Someone holding [elevated access](#elevated-access-break-glass)
right now is flagged with when it ends. A model a subject has no access to is left out.

Every answer comes from the panel's own permission resolver, through the same calls a
page makes, so a panel's `has_<verb>_permission` hooks, read-only mode, a custom
`VANTAGE["PERMISSIONS"]` class, authentication backends and field permissions are all
reflected. The report cannot describe a rule the panel does not apply.

**By role** reviews each role as a person holding only that role. A panel hook that
decides from something else about the user (an email domain, say) answers for that
stand-in, so the per-person report is the one to hand over as evidence.

### Downloading

The screen offers **Download CSV** and **Download JSON** for the current view (by person
or role, all models or one). Each download writes an `access-review.export` entry to the
audit log. CSV cells are protected against formula injection: a role named
`=HYPERLINK(...)` is written as `'=HYPERLINK(...)`.

The same report from a shell, for a scheduled export to an evidence store:

```bash
python manage.py vantage_access_review --format csv --output review.csv
python manage.py vantage_access_review --format json --by role
python manage.py vantage_access_review --model shop.order --model shop.customer
```

| Option | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `--format` | `csv` | `csv` or `json` |
| `--output` | standard output | file to write |
| `--model` | every registered model | `app_label.model`; repeat for several |
| `--by` | `user` | `user` or `role` |

The JSON carries `generated_at` and `version` (the package version) beside the subjects.
CSV columns: `subject_type, subject, superuser, elevated_until, model, field, view, add,
change, delete, field_visible, field_editable, field_sensitive, field_reveal`. A row
with an empty `field` is the model itself. `field_reveal` is `per-record` when a panel's
`can_reveal` hook needs a record to answer.

### Who may open it

Superusers. `VANTAGE["ACCESS_REVIEW_PERMISSION"]` widens it to a permission string or a
callable taking the request. It is code-only: the report names everyone who holds the
keys to the panel.

### What it does not show

Row-level scoping (tenants, object permissions) decides *which* records someone sees,
not whether they see the model, and is not in the report. Neither are permissions your
own code checks outside the panel.

## Elevated access (break glass)

A role, or named permissions, held for a few minutes with a stated reason, instead of
standing admin rights.

### Asking and granting

**System → Elevated access** is open to every staff member:

- **Request** elevated access for yourself: a role and/or permissions
  (`shop.change_order`), a duration and a reason of at least ten characters. It waits
  until someone allowed to grant approves it.
- **Grant** it to someone directly, or **approve** a waiting request, if you may grant.
- **Revoke** an active grant, or **reject** a request. Anyone can end their own.

Who may grant is `VANTAGE["BREAK_GLASS_PERMISSION"]`: superusers by default, or a
permission string or callable. Code-only, like `ROLES_PERMISSION`. The roles screen's
rule applies: **a granter who is not a superuser can only grant permissions they hold
themselves**, counting their standing permissions only. Elevation never counts towards
granting more of it or towards editing roles.

Nobody approves their own request unless `VANTAGE["BREAK_GLASS_SELF_SERVICE"]` is
`True`. Then anyone allowed to grant may activate their own request at once, beyond
their standing permissions. That is the point of the switch, for an on-call rota whose
members are named by `BREAK_GLASS_PERMISSION`. The reason, the cap and the audit trail
bound it.

Every grant lasts at most `VANTAGE["BREAK_GLASS_MAX_MINUTES"]` (60 by default). Longer
requests are refused, and approval clamps to the cap in force at that moment. Grants
cannot go to superusers (they already hold everything) or disabled accounts.

### What it gives

While a grant is active, its holder has the role's permissions (and its votes in
[field permissions](field-permissions.md)) or the named permissions, everywhere the
panel checks: pages, actions, exports, the [JSON API](api.md), a background job's
re-check before it runs, and the reveal permission for sensitive fields. It never sets
`is_superuser`, and it only ever widens: a role whose field rules are stricter than
yours cannot hide what you could already see. [Tenant](tenancy.md) scoping still
applies in full.

**Nothing is written to group membership, and no job removes anything.** Whether a
grant is active is computed from the clock each time a permission is checked, and
cached for one request only. An expired or revoked grant gives nothing from the next
request on.

While elevated, a banner across every page names what is held, when it ends and how
many minutes are left, with a **Drop elevation** button.

### The audit trail

Each step writes an entry (`action_name`) to the [audit log](security.md):
`break-glass.requested`, `.granted`, `.activated`, `.used` (once per permission a grant
actually decided), `.expired`, `.revoked`, `.rejected`, `.dropped` and `.withdrawn`.
Activation and expiry are recorded by whichever check first observes them, exactly
once. Opening the Elevated access screen or running `vantage_break_glass list` records
expiries nobody has observed yet.

### From a shell

For an emergency in which nobody who could grant is reachable:

```bash
python manage.py vantage_break_glass grant ada --role "Order admins" \
    --minutes 30 --reason "Refunds stuck after the payment provider outage" --by root
python manage.py vantage_break_glass grant ada --perm shop.change_order --minutes 15 \
    --reason "Correct one mistyped order total"
python manage.py vantage_break_glass list          # active and pending; --all for every grant
python manage.py vantage_break_glass revoke 12 --reason "Incident closed"
```

Shell access is already beyond anything the panel restricts, so the command does not
check *who* may grant. The reason, the target and the duration cap are still enforced,
and every grant and revocation is audited (`--by` names the actor).

### Limits

- Code that calls `user.has_perm` directly, outside the permission layer, does not see
  an elevation. That includes your own views and a navigation item's own `permission`.
  The panel's resolver, a page's `permission` string and the reveal checks do.
- Django's own admin and other apps never see it: elevation is the panel's.

---

URL: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/django-vantage/two-factor/

# Two-factor sign-in

After the password, a six-digit code from an authenticator app on the person's phone —
Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, 1Password, Bitwarden, or any other app
that does time-based codes (TOTP, [RFC 6238](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238)).
A leaked or guessed password is then not enough on its own.

It needs no configuration and no extra package. Everyone with panel access can switch it
on for themselves from their account page; you can require it of superusers, or of
chosen [roles](roles.md), with one setting.

```bash
python manage.py migrate   # two small tables: the authenticators, and the recovery codes
```

## Setting it up

From **Your account → Set up two-factor sign-in** (`<panel>/_/account/two-factor/`):

1. **Set it up** shows a QR code, the same key written out for typing in by hand, and an
   `otpauth://` link for an authenticator app on the same device.
2. Scan it, then type the code the app shows. Nothing is switched on until a code proves
   the app really has the key — a QR code that was never scanned cannot lock anyone out.
3. Ten **recovery codes** are shown, once. Each signs in once without the phone. Keep them
   in a password manager.

From then on, signing in through the panel's own sign-in page (`vantage.authviews`)
asks for a code after the password. One box takes either an app code or a recovery code.

Turning it off, replacing the recovery codes, or adding or removing an authenticator asks
for a current code (or a recovery code) or the password first.

## Several authenticators

A person can have up to five authenticators at once — a phone and a spare, or a phone and
a tablet — each with a name they choose ("Phone"; blank means "Authenticator"). The
account page lists them with when each was added and last used.

- **Adding one**: type a name, confirm it is you, then scan the new QR code and type the
  code it shows, exactly as for the first. Nothing changes until that code is right. The
  recovery codes stay as they are; no new set is shown.
- **Signing in**: a code from *any* of the person's devices is accepted, and so is a
  recovery code. The session remembers which device passed.
- **Removing one**: use **Remove** on its row of "Your devices" and confirm it is you.
  Each section of the page (remove, add, new recovery codes, switch off) asks for that
  proof itself. A session that removes the device it signed in with, proving it with a code
  from another device or a recovery code, stays signed in; with only the password it is
  asked for a code again. Sessions that signed in with that device
  stop being trusted and are asked for a code again; sessions that used another device
  carry on. Removing the *last* one switches two-factor sign-in off, as before (a role
  that requires it sends the person to set it up again), and deletes the recovery codes.
  **Switch off** removes every device at once.
- **Recovery codes are the person's, not a device's.** They survive removing any one
  device, and a recovery code works whichever devices are left.

Every device keeps its own sealed secret, its own "already used" step (so one device's
code being spent does not spend another's) and its own lockout counters.

Existing accounts need nothing: the migration keeps each person's authenticator, names it
"Authenticator", and attaches their recovery codes to the person.

The QR code is drawn by the package itself (`vantage.qr`), as inline SVG, black on white
in both themes — a phone camera reads that reliably, and the inverted version unreliably.

## Requiring it

```python
VANTAGE = {
    "TWO_FACTOR_REQUIRED_SUPERUSERS": True,
    "TWO_FACTOR_REQUIRED_ROLES": ["Finance", "Support leads"],
}
```

Someone it applies to who has not set it up is sent to the set-up page before anything
else in the panel: every other page, the JSON API and autocomplete refuse until they have.
The requirement takes effect on sessions that are already signed in, not only at the
next sign-in.

**Whoever enrols first owns it.** Setting it up needs only a signed-in session, so for an
account that has not enrolled yet, the password is still enough to enrol — and whoever
does it first holds the account's second factor from then on, its owner included. When
you switch a requirement on, an attacker who already has someone's password can race the
owner to the set-up page. To keep that visible and undoable:

- Every step is in the [audit log](permissions.md#the-audit-log) against the account:
  `two_factor.started`, `two_factor.enabled`, `two_factor.disabled`, `two_factor.codes`,
  `two_factor.recovery_used` and `two_factor.reset`, and for extra devices
  `two_factor.device_started`, `two_factor.device_added` and `two_factor.device_removed`,
  with the address and browser of the request that did it. Device names are recorded;
  secrets and codes never are.
- **Two-factor sign-in for everyone** shows when each person's authenticator was last
  set up. If someone does not recognise theirs, or cannot sign in because "their"
  authenticator is not on their phone, a superuser resets it and they set it up again.
- Ask people to enrol *before* you require it, and confirm on that screen that everyone
  you expect is there.

The requirement covers the panel. If `django.contrib.admin` is mounted too, see
[Django's admin](#djangos-admin) — its own sign-in asks for the password only.

| Key | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `TWO_FACTOR` | `True` | `False` removes the feature entirely, including for people who had set it up |
| `TWO_FACTOR_REQUIRED_SUPERUSERS` | `False` | Require it of superusers |
| `TWO_FACTOR_REQUIRED_ROLES` | `[]` | Require it of members of these roles (`auth.Group` names) |
| `TWO_FACTOR_ISSUER` | `None` | The name in the authenticator app. `None` means `SITE_TITLE` |
| `TWO_FACTOR_MAX_ATTEMPTS` | `5` | Wrong codes in a row before the second step locks |
| `TWO_FACTOR_LOCKOUT_SECONDS` | `300` | How long the first lock lasts; each lock in a row after it lasts twice as long, up to a day |

None of these is editable from the settings screen.

## Django's admin

`django.contrib.admin` has its own sign-in page and its own pages, and neither is the
panel's. Someone who signs in at `/admin/login/` (or wherever your admin is mounted)
gets a fully signed-in session that has never answered a code. The panel notices and
sends that session to its second step before showing anything — but Django's admin does
not ask, and lets it in.

To hold the admin to the same requirement, add the middleware after
`AuthenticationMiddleware`:

```python
MIDDLEWARE = [
    # ...
    "django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware",
    "vantage.twofactor.AdminTwoFactorMiddleware",
    # ...
]
```

Every admin page then asks what the panel asks, of the same person. A session that owes
a code is sent to the panel's second step (`<panel>/_/account/two-factor/verify/`), and
one that owes an enrolment to the panel's set-up page, each with the admin page as
`next`; form posts get a 403, and the admin's autocomplete a JSON 403. The admin's
sign-in and sign-out pages stay open. Admin pages are recognised by the marks
`AdminSite` and `ModelAdmin` put on their views, so a renamed or second admin site is
covered wherever it is mounted.

It is opt-in because it changes a page this package does not own. `manage.py check
--deploy` warns (`vantage.W095`) when two-factor sign-in is required of anyone, the
panel is mounted, Django's admin is mounted in the root URLconf, and the middleware is
not installed.

Other login views of your own — a custom one, an API token endpoint — are yours to
gate: a session they sign in is sent to the second step by the panel, and by nothing else.

## When someone loses their phone

- **They have another device**: they sign in with it, remove the lost one on their own
  page, and add the new phone.
- **They have a recovery code**: they sign in with it, add the new phone as a device (and
  remove the lost one), or switch two-factor off and set it up again.
- **They do not**: a superuser opens **Your account → Two-factor sign-in for everyone**
  (`<panel>/_/account/two-factor/people/`) and resets them. The screen lists every
  device. **Reset** on a device removes just that one and leaves the person's other
  devices (and recovery codes) working; **Reset all**, and the `manage.py` command below,
  remove every device and the recovery codes, which switches their two-factor sign-in
  off. Resetting the last remaining device is the same as resetting all. The success
  message says how many devices were removed, and the reset is recorded in the
  [audit log](permissions.md#the-audit-log) under the superuser's name.
- **The only superuser has lost theirs**: on the server,

  ```bash
  python manage.py vantage_two_factor_reset <username>
  ```

  which removes all of that account's devices and is audited with no actor — the log's
  way of saying "from the command line".

Only superusers can reset someone else, not whoever may manage roles: switching off a
superuser's second factor is a step towards becoming one. A superuser can reset another
superuser's two-factor sign-in without that person's password; that is by design, and
it is audited under the acting superuser's name. Nobody can reset their own from
that screen; their own page asks for proof.

## Upgrading

Migrations `0024` and `0025` move recovery codes from the device to the person. Reversing
them restores the column and points each code at its owner's oldest device; codes of a
person who has no device by then cannot be attached to one and are deleted. Back up
before migrating backwards.

## Safety properties

**Half signed in is not signed in.** After a right password the panel's sign-in does
*not* call Django's `login()`. The session stays anonymous, holding a five-minute note of
who got the password right, so nothing in the project — not only the panel — treats
them as signed in. The note is void if the password changes, the account is deactivated
or the authenticator is removed in the meantime.

**Every panel route is behind the gate.** It wraps every URL a site builds — routes
grouped under an `include()` as well, all the way down — so new pages, plugin pages,
dashboards and the API are covered without opting in. A session signed in through a
*different* login view, such as `django.contrib.admin`'s, is sent to a second-step page
before the *panel* shows it anything; that other view's own pages are not covered unless
you install [`AdminTwoFactorMiddleware`](#djangos-admin) (for Django's admin) or gate them
yourself. Pages are redirected; form posts get a 403; the API and autocomplete get a JSON
403 with `"two_factor": "verify"` or `"enrol"`.

**The session key rotates** when the password is accepted and again when the code is,
so a session id planted beforehand never ends up signed in.

**A code works once.** The 30-second step it was accepted for is stored, and the next
code must be for a later one. Two requests racing with the same code cannot both win: the
check and the update are one conditional `UPDATE`. Codes from one step either side of now
are accepted, for phone clocks that drift; all three candidates are compared in constant
time.

**Wrong codes count against the account, not the session.** The count is kept per device,
but a guess is not free on the others: every wrong code or password is counted against
*each* of the person's devices that is not locked, before it is compared, and counts for
as many attempts as there are such devices. A code is compared against every one of their
secrets, so with `n` devices the second step locks after `ceil(TWO_FACTOR_MAX_ATTEMPTS / n)`
wrong answers (at least one); the chance of guessing a code within one lockout is then no
higher than with a single device. A device that is locked is not compared against at all;
the others still answer, and a right answer starts the counts again on all of them. The
second step as a whole is locked when every device is. Five in a row (by default) lock the second step for five minutes — the right code and recovery codes included — and
throw away the half-signed-in note, so carrying on means typing the password again.
Opening fresh sessions buys an attacker nothing, and neither does sending guesses in
parallel: each attempt is counted, by one conditional `UPDATE`, *before* its answer is
compared, so however the requests interleave no more than five answers are looked at per
lockout. App codes, recovery codes and the password on the "switch it off" form all go
through that same count.

**Each lock in a row lasts twice as long.** Five minutes, then ten, twenty and so on, up
to a day, until a right answer starts the count again. A fixed lock only sets a steady
guessing rate — five tries every five minutes is over a thousand a day, which a six-digit
code does not survive for long — while doubling holds an attacker who has the password
to a handful of guesses a day. A person locked out for longer than they can wait asks a
superuser for a [reset](#when-someone-loses-their-phone). The password step keeps its own
[throttle](security.md#loginthrottlemiddleware).

**The secret is sealed and shown only once.** It is encrypted at rest with a key derived
from `SECRET_KEY` (HMAC-SHA256 in counter mode, then a separate HMAC-SHA256 tag, so a
tampered row is refused rather than decrypted to something else). The tag also covers
whose secret it is and which enrolment, so someone who can write to the table but not
read `SECRET_KEY` cannot copy their own sealed secret over a colleague's and answer for
them with their own phone. A copy of the database alone does not reproduce anyone's
codes. After a code has confirmed it, nothing renders it again. Rotate `SECRET_KEY` the
[documented way](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/settings/#secret-key-fallbacks)
— with the old key in `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS` — or every enrolled person will need a
recovery code or a reset. Each person's secret is sealed again under the new key the
next time they sign in with a code, so once everyone has, the fallback can go; anyone
who has not by then needs a recovery code or a reset. Values written before the binding
existed (`v1$…`) are still read, and are rewritten the same way. Recovery codes are unaffected by the key: they are 80 random
bits each, stored only as their SHA-256.

**Neither table is ever a panel model.** `TwoFactorDevice` and `TwoFactorRecoveryCode` are
in the registry's built-in exclusions, so no generic list, form, export or API exposes
them.

**CSRF everywhere.** Every view here is `csrf_protect`-ed and `never_cache`-d, so it holds
even in a project that has removed `CsrfViewMiddleware`. Pages that show a secret or
recovery codes are sent with `Cache-Control: no-store`.

**Impersonation does not touch it.** The gate asks about the person at the keyboard, not
the account being impersonated, and a superuser's proof survives starting and stopping
impersonation. The set-up and reset screens refuse while impersonating.

## The `manage.py check` messages

| Id | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `vantage.E095` | `TWO_FACTOR_REQUIRED_SUPERUSERS` is not a bool, or `TWO_FACTOR_REQUIRED_ROLES` is not a list of role names |
| `vantage.E096` | `TWO_FACTOR_ISSUER` is empty, not a string, or contains a colon |
| `vantage.E097` | Two-factor sign-in is on and the panel is mounted, but no `SessionMiddleware` is installed |
| `vantage.W095` | `--deploy` only. Two-factor sign-in is required of someone, and `django.contrib.admin` is mounted without [`AdminTwoFactorMiddleware`](#djangos-admin) |

## Limitations

- **Five authenticators per person.** A cap, because each one is another place a code can
  be guessed against.
- **A new role membership reaches a live session within a minute.** Whether someone has
  an authenticator, and whether a role requires one, is kept in their session and
  re-read at least once a minute — and at once when the requirement settings change.
  Removing a device, a reset and switching two-factor off do not wait for that: each
  request checks, with one indexed query, that the device its session passed with still
  exists, so they take effect on the next request.
- **A device you started but did not confirm expires after ten minutes.** Its secret is
  discarded and the next visit to the page starts a new one.
- **Only the panel is gated, unless you say otherwise.** A session signed in through
  another login view can still use the rest of your project before it answers — Django's
  admin included, until [`AdminTwoFactorMiddleware`](#djangos-admin) is installed. The
  panel's own sign-in, by contrast, signs nobody in until the code is in.
- **TOTP only.** No SMS (deliberately: it is phishable and SIM-swappable), no WebAuthn
  security keys yet.

## See also

- [Security](security.md) — the sign-in throttle and the rest of the hardening
- [Roles](roles.md) — the groups `TWO_FACTOR_REQUIRED_ROLES` names
- [Settings](settings.md#two-factor-sign-in) — every key in one table

URL: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/django-vantage/single-sign-on/

# Single sign-on and role mapping

Vantage signs people in through Django's own authentication, so any SSO library that
logs a user into Django logs them into the panel: [mozilla-django-oidc], [django-allauth]
and [python-social-auth] all work against Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD), Okta, Google
Workspace, Keycloak and other OpenID Connect providers.

What those libraries do not know is which of *your* roles a person's directory groups
should mean. `VANTAGE["ROLE_MAPPING"]` is that mapping, applied on every sign-in.

```python
VANTAGE = {
    "ROLE_MAPPING": {
        "CLAIM": "groups",          # the ID-token claim listing the person's groups
        "MAP": {
            # provider group (name or object id) -> Vantage role(s), i.e. auth.Group names
            "panel-finance": "Finance",
            "panel-admins": ["Support", "Finance"],
        },
        "SET_STAFF": True,          # mapped people get is_staff; unmapped people lose it
        "REMOVE_UNLISTED": True,    # drop managed roles the provider stopped asserting
    },
}
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `CLAIM` | `"groups"` | Where the provider puts the groups. A list, or a space/comma-separated string |
| `MAP` | `{}` | Provider group to one role name or a list of them |
| `SET_STAFF` | `False` | Grant `is_staff` to anyone mapped to at least one role and remove it from anyone mapped to none. Superusers are never touched |
| `REMOVE_UNLISTED` | `True` | Remove a managed role at sign-in when the provider no longer asserts a group that maps to it |

## The rules

- **Only roles named in `MAP` are managed.** A role given by hand that the mapping never
  mentions is left alone, so switching SSO on does not strip an emergency account.
- **Removal follows the directory.** Taking someone out of a group removes the role at
  their next sign-in; off-boarding in the directory is off-boarding in the panel.
- **Never a superuser, never a new role.** A role name in `MAP` that does not exist is
  logged (`vantage.identity` logger) and skipped rather than created empty.
- **Audited.** Every change is an audit entry on the user ("Roles synchronised from the
  identity provider").

Permissions themselves stay on the roles, edited on the [roles screen](roles.md); the
mapping only decides membership. Two-factor requirements by role
(`TWO_FACTOR_REQUIRED_ROLES`) apply to mapped roles like any other — though with SSO
you will usually enforce MFA at the provider instead.

## Wiring it to your SSO library

=== "mozilla-django-oidc"

    ```python
    # myproject/auth.py
    from mozilla_django_oidc.auth import OIDCAuthenticationBackend
    from vantage.identity import MozillaOIDCRoleMixin

    class PanelOIDCBackend(MozillaOIDCRoleMixin, OIDCAuthenticationBackend):
        pass
    ```

    Point `AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS` at `myproject.auth.PanelOIDCBackend`. With Entra ID,
    enable the `groups` claim in the app registration's token configuration.

=== "python-social-auth"

    ```python
    SOCIAL_AUTH_PIPELINE = [
        # ... the default steps ...
        "social_core.pipeline.user.user_details",
        "vantage.identity.social_auth_pipeline",
    ]
    ```

=== "django-allauth"

    ```python
    # apps.py ready()
    from allauth.socialaccount.signals import pre_social_login, social_account_updated
    from vantage.identity import allauth_sync

    pre_social_login.connect(allauth_sync)
    social_account_updated.connect(allauth_sync)
    ```

Anything else can call `vantage.identity.sync_roles(user, groups)` directly.

[mozilla-django-oidc]: https://mozilla-django-oidc.readthedocs.io/
[django-allauth]: https://docs.allauth.org/
[python-social-auth]: https://python-social-auth.readthedocs.io/

URL: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/django-vantage/sensitive-fields/

# Sensitive fields

[← Index](index.md)

A field that looks like a secret is treated as one before anybody says so. Its value is
masked on every surface the panel has — list cells, the detail page, exports, the JSON
API, search, the audit log — and a person with the right permission can reveal one
value at a time, which is logged.

![An API token masked with a Reveal button](assets/screenshots/masked-light.webp){ .dv-shot .dv-only-light }
![An API token masked with a Reveal button](assets/screenshots/masked-dark.webp){ .dv-shot .dv-only-dark }

```python
@register(Customer)
class CustomerPanel(ModelPanel):
    sensitive_fields = ["api_token", "stripe_customer_id"]  # replaces inference
```

That one line is the whole configuration surface for a model. Leave it out and the
fields are inferred; set it to `[]` to switch masking off for that model.

## What is inferred

A field is sensitive when its **name** contains one of the words below as a whole word,
**and** its **type** can actually hold a secret:

```
password  passwd  pwd  passphrase  secret  token  api_key  apikey  access_key
private_key  client_secret  ssn  social_security  tax_id  iban  account_number
card_number  cc_number  credit_card  cvv  cvc  pin  otp  salt  hash  signature
```

"Whole word" means the name is split on underscores (and camelCase), and the word must
be one or more complete parts of it:

| Name | Masked? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `api_token`, `token`, `stripeApiKey` | yes | contains a whole word from the list |
| `tokenizer_name` | no | `token` is not a whole word here |
| `is_secretary` | no | nor is `secret` |
| `passport_photo_url` | no | personal data, not a credential — nothing in the list matches |
| `token_type`, `pin_attempts`, `password_hint`, `otp_enabled` | no | a trailing `_type`, `_count`, `_attempts`, `_hint`, `_enabled`, `_status`, `_length`… makes it a fact *about* a secret |
| `password_changed_at`, `otp_enabled` | no | a date or a boolean cannot hold a secret |

The types that can hold one are text (`CharField` and its subclasses, `TextField`),
`JSONField`, `BinaryField`, `UUIDField` and numbers. Booleans, dates, relations, files
and anything with `choices` never are.

Two things are sensitive whatever they are called:

- **Encrypted field classes** — any field whose class (or a base class) is named
  `Encrypted…Field`, which covers django-fernet-fields, django-encrypted-model-fields,
  django-cryptography and django-pgcrypto-fields without importing any of them.
- **Django's `User.password`** — always masked, even when a panel's `sensitive_fields`
  leaves it out, and never revealable. There is no screen on which printing a password
  hash is the right answer.

`manage.py vantage_scaffold` writes the inferred list out as `sensitive_fields = [...]`,
so the decision is visible in code review.

### The vocabulary

```python
VANTAGE = {
    "SENSITIVE_PATTERNS": ["...", "nhs_number", "routing_number"],  # extend
    # "SENSITIVE_PATTERNS": ["password", "token"],                  # replace
}
```

A list replaces the built-in words; including `"..."` (or Python's `...`) keeps them.
It is a deployment setting, read straight from `settings.VANTAGE` and deliberately not
editable from the panel's settings screen: a screen that can shorten the list is a
screen that can unmask a column.

## What masking looks like

- `••••••••` — always eight bullets, so the mask's width says nothing about the
  value's length.
- `•••• 4242` for card, IBAN and account numbers (`card_number`, `cc_number`,
  `credit_card`, `iban`, `account_number`), because that is how people tell two cards
  apart — but only when the value has at least ten characters, so four of them are a
  small part of it.
- An **empty** value shows as empty. Whether a customer *has* an API token is the
  useful half of the information, and the half the mask is not protecting.

## Every surface

| Surface | What happens |
|---|---|
| List cells | Masked, with a reveal control. Inference never picks a sensitive field as a column; an explicit `list_display` may, and it renders masked |
| Detail page | Masked, with a reveal control; a password hash gets **Set password** instead |
| Summary bar, stat cards, breakdowns | Never aggregated — a min, max or average is a value, or a bound on one |
| CSV / TSV / JSON export | The same mask as the table; empty stays empty |
| JSON API | `{"value": null, "display": "••••••••", "masked": true}` in lists and records; the schema marks the field `"sensitive": true`; a 409 conflict never shows "theirs" |
| Search, filters, sorting | Never searchable, filterable or sortable — each one is an oracle (see below). Applies to declared configuration too, and `manage.py check` warns (`vantage.W090`) |
| Global search and the ⌘K palette | Never match on a sensitive path, never print one in a result's subtitle |
| Autocomplete | Never searches a sensitive field |
| Inline cell editing | Never offered for a sensitive field |
| Edit form | Write-only (below) |
| Bulk edit | Never offered — one secret on forty rows is forty rows sharing it |
| Duplicate | Not copied; the duplicate page says so |
| Import | The preview masks both sides of a changed secret, a sensitive column is never an upsert key, and the mapping step masks sample values for a sensitive column |
| Audit log and record history | Recorded as "changed — value not recorded", never with the value. Applied again when the log is displayed, so an entry written before a field became sensitive stops printing it |
| Page titles and `__str__` | If a record's `__str__` contains one of its own sensitive values (DRF's `Token` returns the key), titles, breadcrumbs, foreign-key chips, search results, autocomplete, select options and audit labels use `"<Model> #<pk>"` instead |
| Markup | The value is never in an attribute, a `data-` blob or a JSON island — the masked cell carries only the reveal endpoint's URL |

### Why search, filtering and sorting are refused

They do not display the value, but each one answers a question about it:

- **Search** — `?q=sk_live_4f` returning one row says a token starts that way. Repeat
  one character at a time.
- **Filtering** — the row count for `pin = 1234` is a yes/no answer per guess.
- **Sorting** — a page sorted by the masked column, plus one value you know, bisects
  every other one.

So a sensitive path is removed from `list_search`, `list_filter`, `ordering` and
`?sort=` whoever declared it, and `manage.py check` tells you when a declaration was
dropped:

```
vantage.W090: 'search_fields' lists 'api_token', which is a sensitive field on
shop.Customer; it is ignored there.
```

## Revealing a value

A masked value on the list or detail page gets a **Reveal** button for users who may
use it. Clicking it:

1. `POST`s to `<app>/<model>/<pk>/reveal/<field>/` — never a `GET`, which browsers
   prefetch, proxies log and history keeps;
2. fetches the record the way every other view does (scoped by `filter_queryset`, so an
   out-of-reach record is a 404, then checked for `view` at object level);
3. asks the panel's `can_reveal(request, obj, field)` — by default, **superusers and
   holders of `vantage.reveal_sensitive`**;
4. spends one unit of the `reveal` rate limit (30 per 5 minutes per account, enforced
   by the view itself, whether or not the security middleware is installed);
5. writes an audit entry — *"boss revealed api_token on Acme Ltd"* — before the value
   leaves the server;
6. answers `{"value": "...", "expires_in": 30}` with `Cache-Control: no-store`.

The page masks the value again after 30 seconds, when the tab is hidden, and when the
page is left — including into the back/forward cache, whose snapshot would otherwise
keep it.

**Hashes are never revealed**, whatever `can_reveal` says: Django's `User.password`, any
field whose name pairs a hash word with a secret word (`pin_hash`, `api_key_digest`,
`password_hash` — a hashed PIN can be brute-forced in milliseconds), and any value that
turns out to be in Django's `algorithm$…` hash format. A bare `content_hash` is a
checksum, and stays revealable. For a user's password the detail page offers **Set
password**, which uses Django's own `AdminPasswordChangeForm`, needs `change`
permission on that user, and is audited with the value redacted.

### The permission
